This paper introduces a novel federated learning approach for creating deep learning models that can analyze histopathology images across various datasets. The proposed system consists of a central server and multiple client nodes, each representing a different medical institution. The server generates artificial data that mimics real histopathology images and trains a deep learning model using these synthetic images. The server then sends the model to the client nodes, which fine-tune it using their own real data and return the updated model to the server. The server aggregates the models from the client nodes and uses them to create a unified model that can be transferred back to the client nodes. The proposed system was evaluated using a dataset of breast cancer images and demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional federated learning approaches. The results showed that the proposed system achieved a high accuracy of 0.93 and a low false negative rate of 0.15 in detecting invasive carcinomas, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods. In machine learning, we often encounter non-convex optimization problems to train models. A key concept in understanding the behavior of such algorithms is the local convexity of the optimization landscape, which represents the landscape of an objective function after removing a subset of the data. In this study, we establish a local strong convexity condition for the average gradient descent algorithm applied to a regularized logistic regression problem with a non-convex penalty. Specifically, we demonstrate that by removing a sufficiently small fraction of the data, the resulting landscape becomes strongly convex relative to the solution, with a convexity parameter proportional to the inverse of the sample size multiplied by the signal-to-noise ratio. This finding implies that the average gradient descent algorithm achieves a linear convergence rate of O(1/T^2) for the average excess risk, which is the best-known guarantee for this algorithm. Additionally, our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments confirming the linear convergence of the algorithm on real and synthetic datasets. This paper introduces the Electron Correlation Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), a deep learning model that predicts potential functions with many-electron atom correlations. Trained on exact electron densities, eCPNNs can be an efficient alternative to traditional quantum methods for calculating total energies and other properties. We demonstrate this capability by using eCPNN potentials to perform Hartree-Fock and post-Hartree-Fock calculations on a set of atoms from helium to barium, achieving accuracy comparable to that of highly correlated traditional methods. Our results show that even a simple Hartree-Fock treatment using eCPNN potentials yields energies and other properties that closely match the reference values obtained with full configuration interaction or coupled cluster theory. This suggests that eCPNNs have the potential to be used as a starting point for more complex calculations, potentially reducing the computational cost by several orders of magnitude. We also explore the possibility of training eCPNNs directly on total energies, rather than electron densities, and find that this approach can be effective for certain systems. However, this method requires a much larger dataset than training on electron densities. Overall, our findings indicate that eCPNNs can be a powerful tool for accurately modeling the behavior of many-electron atoms. By leveraging the universal function approximation theorem, we discuss the potential applications of this method to other quantum systems and highlight the importance of exploring different neural network architectures and training protocols to achieve optimal performance. Our code is publicly available for download.

This paper presents an end-to-end framework for estimating the 6D pose and semantic segmentation of object instances in image data, using a single image as input. Unlike existing methods that rely on pre-computed object features, our approach leverages a multi-task convolutional neural network architecture that simultaneously generates pose and segmentation information for unseen objects. By training the network using synthetic images with ground truth pose annotations, it can generalize to real-world images without the need for annotated training data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this unsupervised approach by applying it to real-world images, and show that it achieves comparable performance to supervised methods on the Linemod benchmark. Additionally, we evaluate the method's robustness to pose variations and demonstrate its ability to generalize to novel objects not seen during training. Experimental results on the BOP benchmark support the method's ability to generalize to new objects without additional training. We introduce an innovative method called Generalized Anisotropic Graphical Lasso (GAGLASS) to estimate and identify sparse and anisotropic inverse covariance matrices from large datasets. This approach overcomes the limitations of traditional Graphical Lasso by allowing for non-uniform sparsity patterns at a relatively low computational cost. Building upon recent advances in Anisotropic Lasso, our method reformulates the optimization problem as a least-squares minimization subject to linear constraints, achieving comparable performance to Graphical Lasso while providing more interpretable results. We demonstrate the efficacy of GAGLASS through simulations and real-world applications, including the analysis of gene expression data and financial network stability. Our findings show that GAGLASS outperforms Graphical Lasso in terms of accuracy and model simplicity, making it a valuable tool for high-dimensional statistical analysis and machine learning tasks. We also provide a user-friendly R package called RAGLASS to facilitate the implementation of GAGLASS. This package is available on CRAN and can be accessed through the RAGLASS GitHub repository. The evaluation shows that this secure island can prevent various types of attacks, including memory corruption, data tampering, and network exploits, while maintaining high performance and low overhead. The proposed hardware design and secure island architecture can be applied to other multi-domain hardware platforms, such as laptops and desktops. We investigate the challenge of developing robust reinforcement learning policies in the presence of reward function errors. Specifically, we consider a scenario where an agent interacts with an environment that contains a limited amount of corrupted data within a known bound. The goal is to find a policy that is nearly optimal for the true reward function, despite the presence of the bounded corruption. We establish a key insight that the optimal policy can be achieved with an accuracy of $\epsilon$ by utilizing an order of $\epsilon^{-2}$ samples. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Natural Policy Gradient method can achieve a policy accuracy of $\sqrt{K\lambda_{max}T\epsilon^2}$ under certain conditions, where $K$ represents the maximum eigenvalue of the inverse Fisher information matrix, $\lambda_{max}$ is the largest eigenvalue of the action-value function matrix, and $T$ is the total number of interactions. Notably, this result is relevant to our problem because the optimal policy accuracy is proportional to the square root of the corruption bound $\epsilon$. Additionally, we show that the sample complexity of the Natural Policy Gradient method is sublinear with respect to the number of interactions $T$. To further address the challenge of learning from corrupted rewards, we propose a new algorithm called the Corrupted Policy Gradient method, which has a sample complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ and achieves an optimal policy accuracy of $O(\epsilon)$. The proposed algorithm is particularly effective in scenarios where the corruption bound is small. To validate the performance of these algorithms, we conduct numerical experiments on various scenarios, including grid world and stochastic control problems with corrupted rewards. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithms in learning robust policies in the presence of reward function errors. Moreover, we provide a theoretical guarantee that the policy learned by the Natural Policy Gradient method is close to the optimal policy for the true reward function, and the policy learned by the Corrupted Policy Gradient method is close to the optimal policy for the corrupted reward function. The proposed algorithms are publicly available on the Capper repository.

Accurately identifying esophageal tumors in CT scans is crucial for radiation therapy and is typically done manually by radiologists, though this process is time-consuming and prone to errors. We propose an end-to-end deep learning approach called the Esophageal Tumor Segmentation Network (ETSNet) that can automatically identify and outline tumors in CT images. ETSNet utilizes a novel attention-guided multi-scale feature fusion technique that enables the extraction of spatial and contextual information from images. This method is particularly effective because it eliminates the need for pre-segmentation masks and post-processing steps. Evaluating ETSNet on a large dataset of 400 CT scans from the National Cancer Institute, it demonstrated superior performance compared to established segmentation networks, achieving a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.83 and a mean surface distance of 3.93 mm. Furthermore, ETSNet outperformed the current gold standard of manual delineation, with a mean surface distance of 2.55 mm, indicating its potential to enhance radiation therapy planning. Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing, with most existing approaches focusing on flat NER. In contrast, our proposed framework, Holistic NER, simultaneously identifies and organizes all nested entities within a single model, eliminating the need for subsequent Coreference Resolution. We introduce a novel holistic NER model that leverages both entity-level and token-level representations to enhance performance. Notably, our model employs a novel entity-aware self-attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies and entity boundaries. We evaluate our approach on three datasets, achieving significant improvements over state-of-the-art flat NER baselines and comparable results to CRF-based holistic NER methods while being more efficient and flexible. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-CLAPA/Holistic-NER.

This study focuses on enhancing the accuracy of automatic image description systems using visual features and sentence structure. We examine the effectiveness of two approaches: combining low-level visual features to represent an image's semantic content, and utilizing a dependency parser to incorporate syntactic patterns in image descriptions. Additionally, we demonstrate that these techniques can be applied to various description tasks, including image captioning and object detection with textual annotations. Our results indicate a significant improvement in captioning accuracy, with a 10.4% increase in BLEU-4 and 12.5% in METEOR, and a notable improvement in object detection with textual annotations, with a 14.8% increase in BLEU-4 and 10.9% in METEOR. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) effectively enhances Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance by leveraging previously translated segments. However, these approaches are limited in their ability to access vast amounts of monolingual data and online TM resources. In this research, we introduce a novel framework called Monolingual Translation Memory (MTM) that effectively incorporates both translation and monolingual data, as well as TM resources, to create a comprehensive memory bank. By utilizing this memory, our proposed method, MTM-Aug, effectively augmentes the memory by learning to retrieve relevant information from the combined data, and then employs a memory-augmented decoder to dynamically access and integrate the information. Experimental results on WMT 2014 Task English-to-German and IWSLT 2016 Task German-to-English demonstrate that our proposed MTM-Aug model outperforms the baseline NMT system by 1.04 BLEU on the validation set and 1.34 BLEU on the test set, respectively. Moreover, our MTM-Aug model achieves comparable performance to strong baselines, including the use of large-scale pre-trained models, on the WMT 2014 validation set with a score of 28.69 BLEU. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/MTM-Aug.

This paper introduces a novel framework called Meta-Structure Learning (MSL), which tackles the challenge of few-shot learning by identifying a prototypical structure for data classification. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on parameterized models, MSL infers a prototypical structure from a set of support samples and applies it to predict labels for novel target samples. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MSL through two experiments: one in a synthetic dataset and the other in a real-world dataset consisting of handwritten digits, showcasing its ability to achieve high accuracy even with as few as one example per class in each episode. Compared to the baseline method, Episodic Training, MSL achieves significant performance improvements, particularly in the low-shot regime. The framework's ability to discover a prototypical structure is further visualized and analyzed to provide insights into its efficacy. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangsun/MSL.

This paper introduces a novel object detection framework that effectively utilizes contextual information to recognize objects. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on single-image information, we've categorized object detectors into three groups: those that use local context, those that use explicit context, and those that use implicit context. Our proposed framework, Context-Aware Object Detection, assesses the performance of 24 context-aware object detectors on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings reveal that context-aware object detectors significantly outperform baseline models, achieving an mAP of 0.326, which is 0.027 higher than the baseline. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the advantages of context-aware object detectors in handling complex scenes, demonstrating an mAP improvement of 1.5% compared to non-context-aware object detectors. Our code and dataset are openly available on GitHub and GitHub Pages. Additionally, we've launched a Context-Aware Object Detection Benchmark, enabling the evaluation of object detectors using contextual information. This benchmark is accessible at the project's GitHub website.

This study examines the outcomes of kidney transplants from incompatible donors for patients with end-stage kidney disease, who require hemodialysis or a living donor transplant.  Due to incompatibility, these patients face increased risks of transplant rejection, kidney damage, and other complications.  A kidney transplant from an incompatible donor can be performed using immunosuppressive medications, but this may lead to a higher risk of certain cancers and infections.  To assess the effectiveness of such transplants, we compared the outcomes of 104 patients who received incompatible kidney transplants with those of 104 compatible kidney transplant patients, matched for age, sex, and blood type.  The outcomes were measured over a 5-year period following the transplant.  The results showed that incompatible kidney transplants had similar survival rates to compatible kidney transplants, but with a higher risk of rejection and kidney damage.  However, the risk of certain cancers and infections was higher in the incompatible transplant group, but only within the first 2 years following the transplant.  The study suggests that kidney transplants from incompatible donors can be effective, but patients may face increased risks of rejection and kidney damage, and may require closer monitoring.  The study also found that the use of certain immunosuppressive medications, such as mycophenolate, may reduce the risk of rejection and kidney damage. In multiagent learning settings, finding an optimal learning strategy that maximizes payoffs in the presence of unknown opponent behavior is a significant challenge. We aim to develop a learning algorithm capable of achieving a high-paying payoff without relying on explicit communication among the agents. Building on the concept of Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE), we establish a lower bound for the achievable payoff and design a novel learning algorithm that can reach a payoff within a constant factor of this lower bound in a finite number of iterations. Finally, we provide a theoretical guarantee that the algorithm converges to a CCE in polynomial time. This study examines the stochastic SIS epidemic model with delayed diagnosis, where individuals with symptoms wait for a certain period before being tested and confirmed as infected. We analyze the model's basic reproduction number $R_w$ and establish the conditions under which the epidemic will fade or be persistent. Specifically, we find that as the infection rate approaches a certain threshold, the final proportion of infected individuals in the stationary distribution will converge to 1, while below this threshold, this proportion will converge to 0. Numerical simulations illustrate the effects of delayed diagnosis on the epidemic's dynamics. Moreover, we derive the minimum delayed diagnosis period required to prevent the spread of the epidemic. This research provides a foundation for exploring other variants of this model.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the supersymmetric source for deformed Wigner matrices have been proposed. We demonstrate that both approaches yield the same result and can be viewed as variants of the Bajnai-Szegedy construction. This unified framework provides a clear proof that the supersymmetry method remains valid for quasi-Gaussian matrices with rotation-invariant spectral measure. Moreover, this proof extends to matrices with correlated random entries, as long as these correlations are themselves rotation-invariant and of a quasi-Gaussian nature. This achievement is further illustrated by deriving a precise eigenvector correlation formula for deformed Wigner matrices. Additionally, we establish that the supersymmetry method can accurately capture the spectral properties of a specific family of non-Hermitian polycyclic matrices, which exhibit a mix of delocalized and localized behavior within their spectrum. This finding is confirmed through numerical simulations. This work provides a foundation for exploring the spectral properties of a broader range of non-Hermitian matrices using the supersymmetry method. The top quark spin asymmetry in $t$-channel single top quark production has been measured using data from proton-proton collisions at 1.96 TeV, with a total luminosity of 9.7 inverse femtobarns. The analysis focuses on final states with one isolated electron and missing transverse energy, and top quark spin asymmetry is determined through a likelihood fit that considers the kinematic properties of the top quark and its decay products. The measured spin asymmetry is $0.25 \pm 0.09$, which is consistent with the Standard Model prediction of $0.44$. Additionally, upper limits on the ratio of gluon polarization to the spin of a proton are $0.045 \leq \Delta G/\Delta S \leq 0.134$ at a 95% confidence level. These results provide valuable insights into the spin structure of the proton.

We present a novel code for N-body simulations in modified gravity models, specifically tailored for the Chameleon and Galileon cosmology. This code overcomes the limitations of previous approaches by directly integrating the non-linear gravitational field equations, bypassing the need for a proxy potential. It achieves this through a combination of a nested N-body method and a second-order iterative solution for the gravitational field. In comparison to existing codes, our method offers improved accuracy and reduced computational cost. We demonstrate the code's effectiveness by simulating a Chameleon cosmology simulation with $4096^3$ particles, with a mass resolution comparable to that of the IllustrisTNG300-NS simulation. The results show that our code accurately reproduces the Chameleon's cosmological effects, including the suppression of power spectrum on small scales and the formation of a central massive galaxy similar to that found in the IllustrisTNG300-NS simulation. Furthermore, we find that the code's performance is robust across different particle masses and resolutions. The code's scalability is also demonstrated through a $10.7$ billion particle simulation, showcasing its potential for large-scale cosmological simulations in modified gravity models. To validate this approach, we introduce a new task called Natural Language Inference in Conversational Spaces (NLI-CONV-SPACE). By incorporating Natural Language Inference as a key aspect of conversations, our primary goal is to identify whether the generated responses demonstrate a capacity for diversity. To achieve this, we create a dataset called NLI-CONV-SPACE, which involves Natural Language Inference statements that can be supported by various types of evidence. We also develop a method to assess the diversity of responses in conversations through self-questioning, and we present a model that outperforms the baseline by a significant margin in terms of diversity. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach can effectively evaluate the diversity of responses in conversations involving Natural Language Inference by comparing it with a baseline model that prioritizes accuracy over diversity. Deep neural networks excel at image recognition but often struggle with incremental learning, a scenario where a network must adapt to continuous new data while retaining previous knowledge. This task is particularly challenging in the presence of imbalanced datasets, where new data significantly differs from prior knowledge. We propose a novel framework called Adaptive Distillation from Multiple Sources (ADMS) to address this issue by efficiently learning from both old and new data with significant imbalances. ADMS leverages a combination of multi-source adaptive distillation and a memory-augmented neural network to selectively focus on valuable knowledge from both sources. By incorporating a source weight mechanism, ADMS can adapt to new data even when it is scarce, reducing the requirement for a large number of new data. Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of ADMS in handling imbalanced incremental learning scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/ADMS.

This paper presents the first result from a series of experiments at the LHC to precisely measure the CKM angle $\beta$ using $B^0_{s}\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decays. Our analysis utilizes a full LHCb dataset, amounting to 9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity in proton-proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV. We employ resonance and off-resonance $J/\psi\phi$ final states to calculate systematic uncertainties and eliminate background. By comparing $B^0_{s}\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ and $B^0_{s}\rightarrow J/\psi K^+ K^-$ decays, we determine $\beta$ with minimal reliance on theoretical input. Our calculation yields $\beta = 0.381 \pm 0.006 \pm 0.005 \pm 0.001$, where the first error stems from statistical considerations, the second from systematic uncertainties, and the third from modeling of hadronic interactions. This result significantly enhances the current precision of $\beta$ measurements. Furthermore, our findings are consistent with those obtained from other LHC experiments and from tree-level transitions in $B^0_{s}\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ decays. Additionally, we extract the value of $|V_{cd}|$ from semileptonic $D^0$ decays, yielding $|V_{cd}| = 0.425 \pm 0.006 \pm 0.003$, which is the most precise determination to date. This value is in line with those from other experiments and from lattice QCD calculations. Our analysis also provides the first direct measurement of the ratio of hadronic branching fractions $\frac{\mathcal{B}(D^0\rightarrow K^0_K)}{\mathcal{B}(D^0\rightarrow \pi^0_K)}$, resulting in $0.0281 \pm 0.0005 \pm 0.0002$. In cooperative systems, agents work together to achieve shared objectives, which can be viewed as finding a suitable equilibrium in their individual decision-making processes. This concept of equilibrium is particularly relevant in situations where agents make independent, self-serving choices to achieve a common goal, as seen in the execution of tasks within a network. We introduce a novel framework that enables the identification of a specific type of equilibrium, which we call'strongly efficient' (SE), in the presence of task execution under specific connectivity conditions. We demonstrate that when the network topology allows for inter-agent communication, an SE equilibrium exists and can be determined through a process of iterative learning. Conversely, in isolated systems, an SE equilibrium may not exist. We also establish that in dynamic systems, an SE equilibrium can be achieved through a process of adaptation, which is robust to small changes in task execution. Notably, this framework assumes that agents' decisions are influenced solely by their local knowledge, which is limited to the network's connectivity and their own payoffs. This research provides a foundation for exploring SE equilibria in more complex and dynamic cooperative systems. Through numerical examples and theoretical analysis, we illustrate the properties and behavior of SE equilibria in various scenarios, including static and dynamic systems, and examine the impact of network topology and communication on the emergence of SE equilibria. These findings have implications for the design of cooperative systems, particularly those involving task execution, and highlight the importance of considering the interplay between local decision-making and network connectivity. This research also opens up new avenues for investigating cooperative systems, including the study of SE equilibria in the presence of external influences and the development of adaptive algorithms for achieving SE equilibria in dynamic systems. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of cooperative systems and the emergence of equilibrium in complex, dynamic networks. Through this research, we seek to advance the field of cooperative systems and provide a foundation for exploring the intricate relationships between local decision-making, network connectivity, and system dynamics. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of LSKL, showing that it achieves comparable or better performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing computational costs. This paper presents a novel approach to optimizing the performance of mobile data networks by incorporating simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) technology. We develop an innovative model that captures the coexistence of SWIPT-enabled access points (SWIPT APs) and traditional APs in a two-tier wireless communication system. Our objective is to maximize the system throughput while ensuring that each SWIPT AP's energy harvesting capability meets a minimum requirement. We formulate this problem as a mixed-integer optimization model and employ a column generation approach to solve it efficiently. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in achieving high throughput values and verify the benefits of SWIPT technology in mobile data networks. Additionally, we provide insights into the optimal configuration of SWIPT APs and their placement in the network. Our findings indicate that SWIPT APs can be strategically located to maximize the system throughput and that the optimal solution often involves a mix of SWIPT and traditional APs. Moreover, we observe that the energy harvesting capability of SWIPT APs can be optimized to balance the trade-off between high throughput and low energy consumption. Overall, our research highlights the potential of SWIPT technology to enhance the performance of mobile data networks.

Object detection in aerial images is a complex task due to the presence of large-scale objects and varying aspect ratios. Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs) have been widely adopted for this purpose, but they struggle with large-scale objects, leading to inaccurate bounding boxes and classification results. This paper presents a novel approach called Cascade Pyramid Link Module (CPLM) that enhances FPN by introducing a hierarchical feature refinement mechanism. By iteratively refining pyramid links across different scales, CPLM effectively reduces the error propagation effect and enhances the detection performance for large-scale objects. We evaluate our approach on the DOTA dataset and achieve state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin of 2.34% in the validation mAP. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates superior performance on the test set with an mAP of 95.19%. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengmingming/CPLM.

The analysis of multivariate data relies heavily on conditional models, which provide a comprehensive framework for exploring the intricate relationships between multiple variables. A key aspect of this analysis involves understanding the distribution of pairs of variables, which can be achieved through the use of copulas. In this study, we focus on a specific type of bivariate distribution known as the extended skew-t copula, which offers a flexible and parameter-rich alternative to traditional models like the Student-t copula. However, estimating the parameters of this distribution through the method of moments leads to a complex optimization problem, which can be challenging to solve, especially in high-dimensional settings. To address this limitation, we propose an alternative estimation approach based on the efficient score function, which enables us to derive closed-form expressions for the score vectors. This efficient estimation approach has several key advantages, including improved computational efficiency and robustness, as well as the ability to handle large datasets. Through extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate the superiority of this method in terms of both accuracy and speed compared to alternative methods, including maximum likelihood estimation and the generalized method of moments. Furthermore, we showcase the practical applications of this method through the analysis of two real-world datasets. In one case, we examine the relationship between stock prices and trading volumes for a set of major US companies, while in the other case, we investigate the connection between GDP growth rates and inflation rates across a group of developed economies. Our findings reveal a range of interesting and previously unreported relationships between these variables. Overall, this research provides a valuable contribution to the analysis of multivariate data and offers a powerful tool for exploring the complex interactions between multiple variables. By leveraging the efficient score function, we can estimate the parameters of high-dimensional conditional models with greater accuracy and at a lower computational cost. We aim to enhance the effectiveness of Wikipedia articles by tackling a critical challenge in natural language understanding: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). This involves identifying the appropriate meaning of a word in a specific context. To address this, we developed a multi-step approach that leverages both semantic resources and machine learning techniques. Our strategy combines a set of pre-processing methods to enhance context features, followed by a classification step utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). We evaluated our approach using the SemEval-2017 Task 10 Wikipedia Subtask, achieving a notable improvement of 4.5% in accuracy compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we applied our best-performing model to disambiguate all the words in the English Wikipedia, amounting to over 1.7 billion WSD instances. This resulted in a 0.5% increase in accuracy on the test data for the same task. To facilitate future research, we made our data and code publicly available. Additionally, we have already incorporated our disambiguation model into the WikiTools suite of natural language processing tools for the English Wikipedia. These tools can be accessed through the WikiTools website.

In this paper, we introduce a new task called "procedural multimedia discourse understanding" (PMDU), which involves interpreting multimedia instructions that combine written and spoken components. To facilitate this research, we present a large-scale, real-world dataset called "MMDB" consisting of 10,000 video tutorials with accompanying written guides, and demonstrate that deep learning models struggle with this task even when provided with extensive training data. Our findings indicate that current models are not capable of utilizing the benefits of both written and spoken components, and that they perform no better than baseline models when trained on either component in isolation. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new model called "Cross-Modal Fusion" that effectively integrates written and spoken components to improve performance, and demonstrate that it outperforms all previous models by a significant margin, achieving a score of 44.1% on the F1 measure, a 10.4% improvement over the best previous result. Notably, this model is capable of effectively utilizing the benefits of both written and spoken components, and we demonstrate that it can generalize to real-world applications, including a notable 12.5% improvement in accuracy when tested on a real-world procedural task. Our findings provide new insights into the challenges and potential solutions for this complex task, and we hope that this dataset and our results will serve as a foundation for further research in this area. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for maintaining safe and effective communication systems. Researchers often study the spread of malicious information through networks, focusing on identifying critical components that, when removed, prevent the spread of contagions. In this study, we examine the impact of targeted attacks on networks by analyzing the effect of node removal on the spread of information. We propose a new measure, avalanche, to quantify the effect of targeted attacks. Avalanche represents the number of nodes affected when a single target node is removed from the network. We investigate the relationship between avalanche and network structure, as well as its connection to network attack resilience. Our findings reveal that the highest avalanche values are observed at specific, vulnerable nodes, which we term 'attack hubs.' These attack hubs are located at the intersection of high betweenness centrality and low degree centrality. We also identify that attack hubs are more common in networks with a mixture of short and long paths between nodes. Notably, we find that attack hubs are not the same as network hubs, which are typically characterized by high degree centrality. Our results provide new insights into network attack resilience and can be used to inform targeted defense strategies. We illustrate the effectiveness of this approach using both synthetic and real-world networks, demonstrating that removing attack hubs can significantly reduce the spread of malicious information. In contrast, removing network hubs has a less pronounced effect on the spread of information. In contrast, $n$-gram models are a simpler alternative that provide similar performance at a fraction of the computational cost. However, they have a major limitation: they cannot generalize beyond the training data. This approach allows the neural model to learn generalizable language knowledge while the $n$-gram model focuses on capturing local dependencies. By incorporating a new loss function, we can train the models in an alternating manner. Our experiments show that this approach significantly outperforms both standalone models, achieving a 10% improvement in perplexity and a 5% improvement in accuracy on the TREC dataset. This method also generalizes well to out-of-domain $n$-gram data, demonstrating its potential for applications such as text summarization and question answering. A Negative Pressure Room (NPR) is a specialized enclosure designed to prevent the spread of infectious agents by containing airborne pathogens within its interior. The primary goal of an NPR is achieved by maintaining a pressure level below atmospheric pressure, which is typically accomplished through the use of a negative pressure fan in conjunction with a HEPA filtration system. The pressure differential between the inside and outside of the room is regulated by a pressure gauge, which is critical for ensuring the safety of individuals entering the room. However, the pressure gauge used in conventional NPR designs is an electromechanical device that can be prone to mechanical failure, which may go undetected. In such cases, the pressure reading may become inaccurate, potentially compromising the safety of individuals who enter the room. This study presents a design for an NPR that utilizes a digital pressure sensor to accurately monitor and display the pressure level, thereby enhancing safety by providing real-time visual feedback through a display screen located outside the room. The design also incorporates a fail-safe mechanism that automatically seals the room in the event of a mechanical failure of the digital pressure sensor. The proposed design was tested using a simulation model to evaluate its performance under various failure scenarios. The proposed design addresses the limitations of conventional NPRs by providing a reliable and safe means of monitoring and controlling pressure levels. We establish a new characterization of finite-dimensional classical invariant subfactors of a specific type, which supersedes the well-known characterization by Ocneanu's graphs. This new characterization utilizes a reduced unitary fusion ring, and from it, we derive a key implication regarding the existence of classical, hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such subfactors are equivalent to a specific type of combinatorial construction, utilizing finite-dimensional classical invariants, and this construction is both necessary and sufficient. This discovery provides a direct link between classical, finite-dimensional invariant subfactors and unitary fusion rings. Additionally, we show that the dimensions of the subfactors in question are directly related to the eigenvalues of the Haar state on the unitary fusion ring. This relationship is then applied to derive a new upper bound for the global dimension of such subfactors, and this bound is shown to be achieved in the case of a specific type of classical, finite-dimensional invariant subfactors. This new upper bound is $\sqrt{d^2+4d}$, where $d$ is the dimension of the unitary fusion ring. This result is further illustrated by constructing a family of classical, finite-dimensional invariant subfactors of increasing global dimension, with a specific asymptotic behavior. This family of subfactors has a global dimension that approaches $\sqrt{2}$ times the square root of the number of natural units in the unitary fusion ring, as the natural units become infinitely numerous. This finding is relevant to the study of quantum field theory and topological phases of matter. It is also shown that the Haar state on the unitary fusion ring can be approximated by a sequence of subfactor states, and this approximation is both continuous and has a specific asymptotic behavior. This result has implications for the study of quantum systems with long-range interactions. This new characterization of classical, finite-dimensional invariant subfactors also provides a new framework for the study of operator algebras and subfactors. This framework is more general than previous characterizations and can be applied to a broader range of situations. This new framework is also expected to have implications for the study of mathematical physics and quantum field theory. In this research, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which leverages the power of differential equations to optimize parameters for a wide range of tasks. This framework outperforms traditional meta-learning methods by achieving faster adaptation and higher accuracy. Notably, our approach provides an interpretable representation of the adaptation process, capturing the dynamics of an implicit optimization procedure. By comparing our method to both traditional meta-learning and explicit optimization methods, we demonstrate its superiority in terms of speed and performance. The code for our framework is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/ode-maml. Our results show that ODE-based meta-learning can adapt to new tasks at least 2 times faster and with at least 10% higher accuracy compared to MAML on common datasets. Moreover, our approach outperforms both MAML and REWWE on the miniImageNet dataset with a 6.4% higher accuracy after 6000 adaptation steps. Our findings suggest that ODE-based meta-learning offers a compelling alternative to current meta-learning methods. By modeling optimization as a dynamic process, we can unlock the full potential of optimization and adapt to new tasks more effectively. This research opens up new avenues for exploring the connection between optimization and differential equations, and we anticipate that our work will inspire further innovation in the field of meta-learning. The reliability of machine learning models in critical domains relies on their ability to provide consistent and unbiased performance across various scenarios. To ensure this level of trustworthiness, a comprehensive framework is proposed that leverages a diverse range of techniques, including robust training methods, data validation processes, and performance metrics, to be deployed in real-world settings. This proposed framework, referred to as the Trustworthy Machine Learning Framework, incorporates a set of tools that can be applied to enhance the safety and reliability of machine learning models. The framework is particularly suited for evaluating the performance of models in safety-critical domains, such as autonomous vehicles and medical diagnosis systems. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the framework is applied to a case study involving the evaluation of a deep learning-based object detection algorithm, specifically the Faster R-CNN model. The results obtained from the framework reveal that the inclusion of a data validation process significantly improves the performance of the model, resulting in a notable reduction in false positives and an improvement in average precision. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of identifying prohibited items in X-ray images, specifically focusing on detecting dual tasks. Our primary contribution is the development of a novel attention-based module called Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM), which utilizes lateral connection and calculates a difference map to emphasize task distinction and suppress overlapping features. Furthermore, we introduce a DualTask Detection Network (DTDNet) framework that incorporates LIM in a cascaded structure to enhance performance. By incorporating a cascaded LIM module, DTDNet outperforms existing single-task methods on the Anti-Theft Bag X-ray Inspection (ATBXI) dataset, achieving a significant boost in accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method excels in detecting both tasks simultaneously, and we provide a detailed analysis of the module's impact through ablation studies. Moreover, we conduct a case study to visually illustrate the LIM module's ability to focus on task-specific features. Our code and dataset are available online.

This paper introduces the $n$th toroidal colored Jones polynomial, denoted as $J_n^T$, a polynomial in variables $u,v$ that corresponds to the representation of knots in the $n$th copy of the torus's Kauffman bracket spectrum. We establish relationships between $J_n^T$ and the original colored Jones polynomial, as well as its properties, including invariance under the action of the braid group and the ability to determine isotopy classes of knots. Furthermore, we derive a Kauffman bracket theorem for links in the torus, which enables the application of $J_n^T$ to study links in the torus. By analyzing $J_n^T$, we identify a pattern leading to a conjecture about the periodicity of $J_n^T$ for hyperbolic knots. We also explore the relationship between $J_n^T$ and the volume of hyperbolic knots. Notably, we demonstrate that the volume of a hyperbolic knot is bounded by a constant times the logarithm of the absolute value of the $n$th coefficients of $J_n^T$. This discovery provides a new way to estimate the volume of hyperbolic knots. Additionally, we introduce a method to compute the volume of hyperbolic knots using $J_n^T$. By applying this method to a specific family of hyperbolic knots, we are able to demonstrate that their volumes grow exponentially with respect to the crossing number. This finding indicates that the volume of a hyperbolic knot can increase exponentially with the crossing number. This result provides a counterexample to a previously proposed inequality between the volume and crossing number of a hyperbolic knot. This new example also shows that the volume of a hyperbolic knot can grow exponentially with the minimum number of crossings required to represent it in the torus's Kauffman bracket spectrum. This discovery has significant implications for our understanding of hyperbolic knots and their properties. This paper presents a new perspective on the study of hyperbolic knots, offering a fresh approach to analyzing their geometry and topology. This new approach opens up new avenues for research and may lead to further breakthroughs in the field of hyperbolic geometry and topology. This breakthrough has the potential to significantly expand our knowledge of hyperbolic geometry and topology. The signal was distinguished from background with a significance of 3.8 standard deviations, or 3.9 standard deviations when considering only events with two b-tagged jets. This paper introduces a novel approach to generating music playlist descriptions.
It employs a multi-modal model that combines text and audio features to produce
a concise and accurate description.
A new dataset, Music21, is created to facilitate this approach, comprising
10,000 annotated playlist descriptions and associated audio tracks.
In addition, a text-audio fusion model is proposed to leverage both modalities.
Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of this approach over a
baseline model using only text-based information. Furthermore, human assessment
indicates that the proposed model generates more engaging and relevant descriptions. 
The model's ability to incorporate audio information is also confirmed through
analysis of its performance on in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations. 
The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/music21.

This approach offers a direct and efficient means of simulating time-dependent properties of interacting Bose gases in one-dimensional environments. Temporal action detection in videos aims at pinpointing the start and end points of actions occurring within a video. A recent approach known as end-to-end multi-task detection has shown significant promise in this area, but it has a major drawback of relying on frame-level features that are computationally expensive to obtain. In this study, we propose an innovative end-to-end approach that utilizes video-level features to predict action boundaries. By leveraging the semantic information contained in video titles, we develop a method to learn action duration from video titles, which is then used as auxiliary information to guide boundary prediction. Experiments conducted on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14 demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our method achieves a notable improvement of 2.4% in mean average precision (MAP) on ActivityNet v1.3. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric called average precision per second (APS), which provides a more comprehensive understanding of action detection performance. Our approach also exhibits superior performance on the more challenging task of detecting rare actions. Code and models are available at https://github.com/zhengyangsun/End2End-ActionBoundary.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various tasks, yet their knowledge learning capabilities are limited by their own training data. To overcome this, Teacher-Student architectures have gained popularity by leveraging multiple DNNs to share knowledge. Among these, knowledge distillation has become a leading approach, where a student model learns from a teacher model, often utilizing the teacher's probabilistic distribution as supervision. Despite its success, traditional knowledge distillation faces several challenges, including the need for large-scale teacher models and the difficulty of training multiple teacher networks. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel knowledge distillation framework called Adaptive Distillation (AD), which dynamically adjusts the teacher and student networks during training. By iteratively adapting the teacher and student models to each other's current performance, AD achieves superior performance with minimal parameters. Experimental results on image classification and object detection demonstrate that AD outperforms the baseline knowledge distillation methods, achieving a significant improvement of 1.4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet and a 2.4% AP improvement on COCO object detection. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangfang/adaptive_distillation.

This paper presents a novel approach to designing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Notably, our approach enables the design of safe controllers for complex systems with hard input constraints, providing a practical solution for real-world problems. Additionally, we discuss the potential of ICCBFs to be combined with learning-based controllers and highlight the importance of considering hard input constraints in optimal control problems. This paper presents a new approach called penalized predictive control (PPC), a model-free method that builds upon and enhances traditional model predictive control (MPC). PPC addresses the limitations of MPC by incorporating a data-driven disturbance rejection strategy, leveraging historical input and output data to minimize the need for precise system modeling. By directly optimizing a performance criterion, PPC outperforms MPC in terms of performance, without relying on costly system modeling. Theoretical stability guarantees are provided for discrete-time systems, and the paper demonstrates the effectiveness of PPC through simulations and hardware experiments involving a quadcopter and a robotic arm. The accompanying code is available online. By providing a flexible and high-performance solution, PPC can be applied to various linear and nonlinear systems, enabling real-world applications. The approach also offers a new perspective on the role of feedback in control systems. The research is relevant to the broader field of control theory and has implications for the development of future autonomous systems. The authors propose several avenues for further research and potential applications of the PPC method. We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the use of a non-affine parameter along the
timelike direction. We derive the full set of $1/c^2$ corrections to the Einstein
equations of motion, obtaining the leading order as a conformally deformed
Schwarzschild metric. We also examine the effect of a non-constant gravitational
potential on a test particle, finding that the geodesic deviation equation
includes an extra force proportional to the mass of the particle. This force can
be interpreted as the gravitational equivalent of the Lorentz force. We discuss
the possibility of observing the new force through the precession of perihelia
of planets in our solar system. Finally, we discuss the potential for this
framework to provide a theoretical basis for the Brans-Dicke theory of gravity.

Recent advances in high-performance computing, specifically HPC systems, are becoming increasingly complex and difficult to manage due to their dynamic and unpredictable nature. As a result, there's a growing need for automated tuning of these systems to achieve optimal performance. In our research, we've developed a novel approach called Structured Bayesian Optimization that leverages performance models and utilizes probabilistic methods to efficiently identify the best configuration. By combining this approach with a system called HyperTune, we've successfully demonstrated significant performance gains on two prominent HPC applications, VTK and MiniAMR, by achieving a 2.5x speedup on a single node and a 1.5x speedup on a 1024-node system with a 10% energy reduction. Furthermore, our findings indicate that Structured Bayesian Optimization can be applied to a broader range of applications and we're actively exploring ways to integrate this approach with existing tuning frameworks. Our code is available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. By open-sourcing HyperTune, we aim to encourage collaboration and contribute to the advancement of automated HPC tuning.

This study presents a novel approach to analyzing time series data, an approach that diverges from conventional maximum likelihood estimation. By applying a method called spectral likelihood estimation, we can efficiently obtain reliable sample autocorrelation estimates even for complex and high-dimensional time series. This method is particularly effective in modeling and analyzing multi-scale and nonlinear processes. Building on this, we develop a framework to test hypotheses about the spectral properties of these processes, a framework that can be applied to both finite and growing parameter spaces. Notably, our approach enables the construction of confidence intervals for the spectral structure of time series data. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in accurately estimating the spectral properties of time series, including both stationary and non-stationary processes. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical utility of our approach by applying it to two real-world datasets. The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, driven by the growing use of smart devices and applications. As a result, software developers are under increasing pressure to create and test complex IoT applications quickly. However, the testing of these applications is hindered by the lack of a standardized and automated testing framework. In this research, we present a novel approach called IoT-Test, a comprehensive testing framework that addresses the challenges of testing IoT applications by integrating a formal testing method with a machine learning-based performance evaluation technique. IoT-Test consists of three key components: a test generator that creates test cases based on the application's functional and performance requirements, a test executor that runs the generated test cases and collects data, and a performance evaluator that uses machine learning to assess the test results and identify areas for improvement. The effectiveness of IoT-Test is demonstrated through a case study involving a smart home system, where it successfully detects and prioritizes performance issues. The results show that IoT-Test can detect performance problems with an accuracy of over 90% and prioritize them effectively. The framework is designed to be adaptable to various IoT applications and can be integrated into the development process to provide timely feedback to software vendors. Soft-tissue registration is a critical component in medical procedures such as tumor treatment and surgical planning.  Establishing accurate, real-time 3D soft-tissue maps is essential for guiding minimally invasive interventions.  This paper presents a novel approach to non-rigid registration using a convolutional neural network, enabling real-time 3D-to-2D matching from pre-operative MRI and intra-operative ultrasound images. This method has the potential to enhance real-time 3D target localization from 2D ultrasound images, thus benefiting the guidance of minimally invasive interventions. Spiking Neural Networks, inspired by biological neurons, offer a promising alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks. By leveraging their inherent ability to learn from temporal patterns, SNNs can perform computations on individual neurons, thus reducing the need for extensive network connectivity. In this work, we present a novel approach to training SNNs, combining the advantages of both continuous and discrete learning methods. By integrating a dynamic learning rule with a spike-driven learning update, we achieve a significant reduction in training time and a notable improvement in classification accuracy on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Our findings provide a foundation for further exploration of efficient deep learning algorithms inspired by the human brain. By leveraging the unique properties of spiking neurons, we can develop more robust and adaptable models that excel in real-world applications. This study examines the spectral stability of solitary wave solutions in a one-dimensional Klein-Gordon model that includes a periodic potential and variable wave speed. The potential and wave speed must satisfy specific conditions to guarantee the existence of these solitary waves. Our approach involves transforming the Klein-Gordon equation into a new equation with a conserved quantity, which enables us to analyze the linearized equation around the solitary wave solution. We then investigate the spectrum of the linearized equation using a combination of mathematical techniques, including the Fourier transform, properties of the Mathieu operator, and the application of Wronskians. Ultimately, our analysis confirms the spectral stability of the solitary wave solution through a demonstration of non-negativity of a specific invariant measure. This result is further supported by an explicit expression of the Lyapunov exponent, which is consistently zero. This research extends and refines earlier findings from [6, 7] while also providing a more comprehensive framework for understanding the dynamics of these solitary waves. It is worth noting that the proposed method can be adapted for analysis of other types of solitary waves, such as those occurring in the NLS equation with variable potential and wave speed. Additionally, this study provides a foundation for exploring the impact of small amplitude variations in the Klein-Gordon equation on the stability of these solitary waves. This paper investigates a biharmonic Choquard type equation on R^4, where the nonlinearity $f(v)$ is allowed to have a critical growth of order 4.5. We establish the existence of a ground state solution via the Mountain Pass theorem, and our approach involves modifying the argument found in Biehler's work. Notably, our result surpasses the limitation found in Biehler's study, which was restricted to lower growth thresholds of $f(v)$. Additionally, we prove the regularity of the ground state solution and its uniqueness through a uniqueness lemma. Furthermore, we demonstrate the decay properties of the ground state solution, both in the sense of H\"older continuity and the rate of decay in the supremum norm. These findings are achieved through a combination of the regularity lemma of Shataoff and the sharp decay estimate of the ground state solution for the Choquard equation. Lastly, we establish the uniqueness of the ground state solution in the space of ground state solutions with specific decay properties. This uniqueness is established through a comparison argument, utilizing the maximum principle for biharmonic operators and the properties of the ground state solution. We establish a precise equivalence between computable functions and those using a limited number of operations, specifically, alternations between halting and continuous applications, for functions that can be represented by finite automata and continue to do so for regular functions, provided they are one-to-one, onto, or have a computable inverse that is one-to-one, onto, or has a computable inverse. Additionally, this equivalence extends to continuous functions on real numbers using a more expansive set of operations, and it also holds for functions with a computable representation, including polynomials and rational functions, as well as computable functions in the Turing machine sense. Furthermore, we show that using only finite alternations between halting and continuous applications results in a significantly more efficient computation of functions compared to the standard approach, leading to a substantial decrease in the number of steps required. This efficiency gain is demonstrated through a concrete example of computing the square root function. Moreover, we propose a new model of computation called the alternator, which is capable of processing unbounded inputs while maintaining efficient computation, and we show that it is Turing-equivalent to the standard Turing machine model. Finally, we explore the possibility of applying this alternator model to develop efficient algorithms for solving problems related to the structure of finite automata.

We evaluate our dual-MLP architecture on several classification, clustering, and generation tasks for images and videos, and the results show that it achieves superior performance compared to other methods, including those that employ data augmentation and dimensionality reduction techniques. Moreover, our approach exhibits excellent generalization capabilities, outperforming other methods even when tested on unseen datasets. We aim to enhance the cross-task generalization of multi-task language models by leveraging task-agnostic data. To achieve this, we propose a novel framework called Generalized Multi-Task Learning with Retrieval (GMTLR). GMTLR utilizes a retrieval-based approach to select relevant task-agnostic examples during dense retrieval, allowing the model to learn task-agnostic representations that are transferable across tasks. By integrating a contrastive loss function, we enable the model to distinguish between task-specific and task-agnostic information. Through dense retrieval and contrastive loss, the model learns to generalize across tasks from task-agnostic data. We evaluate our framework on the NLP tasks of sentiment analysis, question answering, and text classification, utilizing the Wikipedia dataset. The experimental results demonstrate that our framework effectively enhances cross-task generalization by an average of 3.5% compared to the baseline model. Additionally, we observe that our approach is robust and effective even with a relatively small amount of task-agnostic data. The code is available at https://github.com/chen308/gmtlr.

This study presents novel algorithms for adjusting hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent method, specifically tailored for optimizing a wide range of objectives subject to differential privacy constraints. Building on existing research, we develop two new methods that can efficiently find optimal hyperparameters: a grid search technique utilizing the differential privacy accounting method importances, and a Bayesian optimization approach that incorporates a private surrogate function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms in multiple scenarios, including hyperparameter tuning for machine learning models and resource allocation in power systems. Notably, our results show that the Bayesian optimization method outperforms existing baselines in multiple scenarios, achieving up to 3.5 times improvement in objective function values. We also provide open-source code for the proposed algorithms and demonstrate their applicability to real-world problems, such as optimizing private neural networks and differentially private time series forecasting. Additionally, we contribute a publicly accessible dataset of private hyperparameter tuning experiments, along with a user-friendly interface for designing and optimizing private machine learning models. This interface is available at the Private ML Studio website. The code and dataset are available at the corresponding GitHub repository. This research paper presents LifeStream, a novel data processing framework designed to efficiently handle physiological data streams. Through a case study involving the analysis of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, LifeStream's capabilities are demonstrated, showcasing its ability to execute complex algorithms while minimizing memory consumption. This paper provides the geometric framework for both future and past oriented curves in higher dimensional space, before defining and analyzing a specific type of curve, the Bertrand curve, in these contexts. We establish a new category of curves, the (1,3)-Bertrand curve, characterized by having a curve that intersects it and is not a multiple or a factor curve, while also not being tangent or orthogonal, and this occurs at a specific point in the future direction from the point of intersection. We demonstrate that in a 4-dimensional Euclidean space, a curve cannot be a (1,3)-Bertrand curve. Additionally, we establish conditions and an explicit formula for a curve to be a (1,3)-Bertrand curve in a 5-dimensional Euclidean space. Finally, we explore and compare the characteristics of (1,3)-Bertrand curves in 4-dimensional and 5-dimensional Euclidean spaces.

Deep neural networks are highly effective in supervised classification tasks, but their training requires large labeled datasets. To enhance their performance with limited labeled data and abundant unlabelled data, we introduce a novel approach based on the Swag-Gamma framework. This method utilizes the swag ensemble's predictive variance to guide a gamma process, which in turn forms a semi-supervised loss function. By iteratively refining this loss function, we can efficiently utilize unlabeled data and adapt to new classes. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods on the CIFAR-100 dataset and achieves comparable performance to direct multi-task supervised training on the tiny ImageNet dataset with 20 classes. The code is available at https://github.com/zheng062/ssemi-supervised-learning.

When seeking to improve imitation learning through interactive feedback from a teacher, a significant challenge arises from the high cost associated with gathering this feedback. As a result, the learning process is often hindered by a substantial limitation: the teacher can only provide feedback on a limited number of actions. This problem is further exacerbated by the fact that the teacher's feedback is not always relevant to the actions taken during the learning process. In this research, we address this issue by developing a method to actively select actions for which the teacher's feedback is most valuable. This approach is grounded in the principle of maximizing the expected gain in log-likelihood of optimal behavior, and is demonstrated through experiments to yield superior performance compared to existing methods. Our findings show that our active learning algorithm achieves a notable improvement of 10-20% in accuracy in comparison to passive learning, and outperforms other active learning methods by a margin of 5-15%. Moreover, our approach exhibits robustness in scenarios where the teacher's feedback is noisy. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/chen308/active imitation learning.

Current image deraining techniques primarily rely on supervised learning and utilize artificially created rainy images for training. However, these methods often struggle with real-world rainy images due to the significant difference between artificial and genuine rain patterns. In this research, we introduce a novel image deraining framework that leverages contextual information and utilizes real-world rainy images for training. By combining a contextual prior model and a non-local means filter, our approach effectively reduces the impact of over-saturated pixels on neighboring areas, thereby effectively removing rain from images. Comprehensive evaluations using both artificially created and genuine rainy images demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing techniques. Moreover, our approach achieves superior performance on real-world rainy images without the need for specific weather conditions, thereby showcasing its practical applicability. The source code and training data are available at https://github.com/zhengming_sun/Real-World-Image-Deraining.

We introduce a novel approach to reward learning using unlabelled data and human feedback in the form of related tasks. This approach utilizes the structural connections between tasks in a reward learning graph to effectively incorporate unlabelled data and human feedback. By optimizing a task-specific objective function, we can learn a general reward function that effectively predicts task labels. However, this approach faces significant challenges due to the high dimensionality of action spaces and the limited effectiveness of traditional human feedback methods. To address this, we propose a new human feedback method called 'active reward learning through iterative human evaluation' (ARL-IE), which involves an iterative process of human evaluation and reward learning. In the initial stage, we use a simple unsupervised learning approach to identify the most relevant tasks and learn the reward function. We then select a subset of the most relevant tasks for human evaluation and learn the reward function using reinforcement learning. This process is repeated iteratively until convergence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ARL-IE through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Notably, our results show that ARL-IE achieves a significant improvement of over 50% in accuracy compared to traditional human feedback methods. Additionally, we found that the proposed ARLE framework is robust to various parameters and outperforms other reward learning methods, including those that use human feedback directly. Our findings suggest that leveraging related tasks and using human feedback through ARL-IE can effectively learn a general reward function even with limited human data. The lack of structured commonsense knowledge in artificial intelligence has hindered its real-world applicability. To address this, we introduce ATOMIC, a large knowledge base comprising 312,000+ annotated text segments that convey everyday reasoning. This database is 10 times larger than the next closest set of commonsense knowledge and includes 350 diverse concepts. Our experiments demonstrate that current NLP models struggle to effectively utilize ATOMIC, but we show that our approach can effectively leverage this knowledge to achieve state-of-the-art performance in several tasks, including natural language inference and text generation. Additionally, we find that these models can learn generalizable patterns of reasoning from ATOMIC and apply them to novel scenarios. Sequential neural network models that process sentences one token at a time have achieved significant success in NLP tasks such as part-of-speech tagging, semantic role labeling, and parsing. However, these models are prone to errors when dealing with tasks like predicting grammatical agreement in Basque, which often rely on distant dependencies and require a deep understanding of sentence structure. Our analysis of the SCL task in Basque reveals that sequential models struggle with the following issues: (1) they fail to capture long-distance dependencies typical of SCL in Basque, (2) they are sensitive to the order of subject and complement, and (3) they don't utilize the semantic information of the complement accurately. To address these challenges, we propose a new approach called "Complement-Aware" that incorporates the semantic information of the complement into the subject representation. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains in SCL accuracy across three datasets, including the Basque Tree Bank, and our proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art models by 4.5% on the SCL task in Basque. Furthermore, our analysis of the complement's semantic influence on SCL prediction provides valuable insights into the nature of agreement in Basque. The complexity of modern system configurations necessitates automation in their setup, which in turn accelerates the development cycle through rapid, automated testing and deployment. This paper introduces a novel approach called AutoReconfig, a lightweight, general-purpose tool that automatically generates customized configurations by solving formalized problems. By leveraging satisfiability solvers, AutoReconfig can efficiently find configurations that meet specific requirements across a wide range of systems and protocols, including network protocols, file systems, and database configurations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the configuration of an SDN testbed and a web server cluster, showcasing its ability to create optimal configurations that balance performance and security. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this approach on the development of self-healing and adaptive systems. By combining AutoReconfig with monitoring tools, it can detect and respond to changes in system behavior, further enhancing its capabilities. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems, utilizing the SU(1,1) algebra as a prime example. By classifying all possible irreducible representations of the SU(1,1) algebra, we demonstrate that the operator dimension $\Delta$ is confined within the range $0\leq\Delta\leq 2$, which is determined by the central charge $c$ of the associated conformal field theory. Furthermore, we establish a direct correlation between operator growth and entanglement properties, revealing that the entanglement capacity of the system is maximized at the upper limit of the allowed $\Delta$ values. Additionally, we show that the operator growth exponent is directly related to the central charge $c$, and that it can be determined by the entanglement structure of the system. Specifically, we find that the exponent is equal to $1$ for $c>0$, and that it is influenced by the presence of Lie symmetry, resulting in a more gradual operator growth compared to systems without Lie symmetry. Notably, we observe that the presence of Lie symmetry also leads to a hierarchical structure in the entanglement spectrum, with distinct levels corresponding to different irreducible representations of the algebra. These findings provide new insights into the operator growth phenomenon and its connection to entanglement, and may have implications for the development of quantum field theories with Lie symmetry. Moreover, we propose that the hierarchical structure of the entanglement spectrum could serve as a diagnostic tool for identifying Lie symmetry in quantum systems. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this research in the study of quantum systems with Lie symmetry, and outline directions for future investigation.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning, enabling the efficient acquisition of complex tasks from human demonstrations. Current imitation learning methods, however, are often confined to single-task settings due to the difficulty of transferring skills across tasks with different action dynamics. To address this challenge, we introduce a framework that leverages kernelized movement primitives to represent robot skills as continuous trajectories in a feature space. By generalizing imitation learning to multiple tasks using Gaussian mixture models, our approach enables the transfer of skills across different action dynamics. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by teaching a robot to perform a task in two different scenarios: (1) learning from human demonstrations in a virtual environment and (2) learning from human demonstrations alongside a robot teacher in a real-world setting. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning algorithms in both scenarios. Moreover, we show that our method facilitates the seamless transfer of skills across different action dynamics, action speeds, and even to a different robot platform. The code for our framework is available at https://github.com/robot-learning/kernelized-imitation-learning.

We introduce a novel approach to generating coherent and detailed narratives in the style of role-playing game (RPG) session summaries. This method involves creating a computer program that simulates a collaborative storytelling experience between human players and a virtual Dungeon Master (DM). This virtual DM is represented by a deep generative model, which produces descriptive passages in response to input from the computer program. These generated narratives are then assessed for their coherence and similarity to actual RPG session summaries. Our evaluation indicates that our virtual DM can effectively engage in creative dialogue with humans, as evidenced by the high correlation between human-generated and machine-generated action histories. Furthermore, our findings show that the virtual DM's narrative skills are comparable to those of human players, as demonstrated by a study in which participants were unable to distinguish between human-generated and machine-generated session summaries in a survey. This suggests that our virtual DM can generate coherent and human-like narratives in RPG settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/nyucl/virtual-dm. Our virtual DM was also incorporated into the open-source platform https://github.com/nyucl/parlor for collaborative storytelling.
