By leveraging a pair of generative models working in tandem, DISCO creates artificial counterfactual instances that are indistinguishable from real data, and then uses these instances to refine the model through a process of iterative correction. Compared to existing methods, our experiments demonstrate that DISCO achieves superior performance in both generating high-quality counterfactual data and improving the accuracy of machine learning models, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. The code for our framework is available on GitHub at https://github.com/chenyong77/DISCO. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the 13th International Conference on Machine Learning and Optimization (ICML 2021).

Heart disease diagnosis heavily relies on cardiac auscultation, a non-invasive technique that uses a stethoscope to identify heart sounds through the chest. Accurate detection of abnormal heart sounds from acoustic signals is critical in diagnosing and treating heart conditions. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages a deep learning technique called dilated convolutional neural networks (DCNN) to automatically identify pathological heart sounds from acoustic signals. Unlike conventional approaches that focus on specific feature extraction, this method directly learns from raw acoustic signals, achieving high accuracy in detecting pathological heart sounds. Our results show that the proposed DCNN model outperforms existing techniques, demonstrating excellent performance in detecting abnormal heart sounds from acoustic signals. This approach exhibits great potential for developing automated systems to aid in heart disease diagnosis and treatment. Moreover, the code is openly available for replication and further research. Additionally, a user-friendly web application has been created to facilitate access to the developed system. This application can be accessed at https://heart-sound-detection.herokuapp.com/. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/AbdullahAlfarsoony/Heart-Sound-Detection.

This framework is comprised of three key components: a wearable health application utilizing Bluetooth Low Energy for data transmission, a cloud-based data aggregation system utilizing attribute-based encryption for secure data sharing, and a cloud-based personalization service utilizing multi-cloud computing for efficient and secure computation. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a case study of wearable electrocardiogram devices, showcasing its effectiveness in providing secure data aggregation and personalized diagnosis while minimizing computational costs. The proposed framework is also evaluated in terms of security, performance, and energy efficiency. The results of this evaluation indicate that the proposed framework achieves a high level of security, efficient computation, and satisfactory energy efficiency. The search for leptoquark particles, which can facilitate rare processes like neutrinoless double beta decay, is being explored through the production of leptoquark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This study focuses on the case of asymmetric leptoquark pair production, where one leptoquark is detected and the other is neutrally lost. Using the ATLAS detector's data from proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and 13 TeV, we simulate the detection of leptoquarks in final states with a top quark and a charged lepton, considering various leptoquark flavors and masses. Our analysis reveals that the discovery of leptoquarks in this scenario is feasible with an integrated luminosity of 300 fb^-1 at 13 TeV, and that the neutral leptoquark can be distinguished from its charged counterpart in certain cases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the neutral leptoquark's coupling can be measured with a precision of 0.02-0.05, contingent on the leptoquark's mass and the available data. This study also highlights the potential for this process to constrain the parameter space of leptoquarks in the context of the type-I seesaw model. As a result, we anticipate that the search for leptoquarks in this process will be a significant area of investigation at future colliders. Temporal sequence analysis in high-dimensional spaces poses significant challenges due to the large number of dimensions and the complex, non-linear relationships between them. Traditional methods often rely on pre-processing techniques to extract local patterns from individual features, thereby losing the underlying structure of the data. To overcome these limitations, we propose a supervised learning approach called Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), which utilizes temporal and spatial information to build a topographic map. By leveraging the temporal and spatial relationships in a growing neural network, SGTM-TT identifies the underlying structure of temporal sequences and detects the dynamic formation of patterns over time. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in discovering latent patterns and classifying sequences. Moreover, the learned topographic map provides valuable insights into the temporal evolution of patterns, enabling us to identify the formation of patterns and their temporal dependencies. By integrating SGTM-TT with a density-based clustering algorithm, we develop a method to cluster temporal sequences based on their dynamic patterns, achieving superior clustering performance compared to traditional methods. The code for SGTM-TT is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/SGTM-TT.

This study introduces a novel hierarchical approach for learning new classes of musical instruments from only a handful of examples. By combining prototypical learning with a hierarchical structure, our method successfully reduces the complexity of the problem by breaking down the task into a series of nested classification tasks. This hierarchical framework enables the effective classification of categories like'string instruments' and 'wind instruments', as well as the precise identification of specific instruments like 'violin'. Our approach achieves superior performance on the MuSound dataset in the few-shot learning setting, outperforming non-hierarchical methods by a significant margin. The primary hurdle for contemporary Question Answering models when analyzing academic papers lies in their limited domain knowledge, which often relies on general-domain knowledge bases and lacks specific knowledge from the scientific community. To address this challenge, our proposed framework, QADoc, leverages the semantic structure of Wikipedia documents to integrate domain-specific knowledge and enhance Question Answering performance. By utilizing a Document Semantic Structure Encoder, QADoc incorporates a semantic structure-aware Wikipedia knowledge base that informs a Question Answering module through attention mechanisms. Experimental evaluations on the S2QA dataset demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing models and achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art models that incorporate external knowledge through memory-augmented neural networks. Moreover, we show that our framework's domain knowledge generalizes across different academic papers, enabling it to effectively answer questions for previously unseen papers. Additionally, we present a visualization of the semantic structure-aware Wikipedia knowledge base and provide insights into the learned representations through both qualitative and quantitative analyses. By successfully integrating domain-specific knowledge, QADoc sets a new benchmark for Question Answering models in the academic domain. The code and data are available at https://github.com/bojunhu/QADoc.

Topological insulators are characterized by exceptional conductivity in one dimension and high electrical resistance in another. This phenomenon occurs due to the presence of edge states within a material's structure. In this study, we investigate a one-dimensional topological superconducting chain made of Rashba semiconductors and demonstrate that the presence of a magnetic field can induce the reversal of the time-reversal symmetry of these semiconductors. Notably, this phenomenon enables the creation of stable zero-energy modes within the gap of the Rashba semiconductors, which can be manipulated through the application of external magnetic fields. This discovery offers a novel approach to designing topological photonic devices using magnetic field control. Additionally, we propose an experiment to observe the time-reversal symmetry breaking and zero-energy modes using microwave cavity resonators. This study provides a promising framework for the development of topological quantum computing and quantum simulation. It also offers a potential solution to the challenge of creating stable zero-energy modes in topological systems. This research can be further expanded to study the dynamics of zero-energy modes in interacting systems. Although it enhances resolution without doubling frame rates, it causes issues with video playback. To address this, we've developed a method to convert interlaced videos into purely progressive content using a single image per frame. Our approach leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) to achieve this conversion, and we've created a comprehensive dataset of 1000 interlaced videos for training and testing our model. When applied to this dataset, our interlaced-to-progressive (I2P) GAN outperforms existing methods and demonstrates a notable improvement in accuracy. This study compares the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. We utilize a simplified model of the left ventricle to demonstrate the BDDC and AMG solvers, and examine how these solvers perform on different scales using up to 1024 CPU cores. Notably, our results demonstrate that the BDDC method can solve a single 3D nonlinear heart simulation in under 18 minutes on 1024 CPU cores. This research aims to inform the selection of suitable preconditioners for cardiac mechanics simulations, particularly for large-scale and nonlinear cases. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. A well-calibrated model effectively predicts its own uncertainty, which is vital in high-stakes applications where decisions are made with limited human oversight. In this paper, we present a novel framework that utilizes a dual-learning approach to achieve confidence calibration. By defining a dual problem that optimizes the inverse of the original model, we can iteratively refine both the model and its inverse until convergence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by successfully calibrating multiple machine learning models, including linear models, decision trees, and neural networks, on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results show that this dual-learning approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in confidence calibration. Moreover, we found that this method not only improves the calibration of the original model but also enhances its overall accuracy. We also provide a Python implementation of this framework as part of the DeepCalib library, which is available on GitHub. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence of this dual-learning approach in the supplementary materials. Our results suggest that this method is robust and can be applied to a wide range of machine learning models. Moreover, we observed that the time complexity of this method is relatively low, making it a computationally efficient solution for large-scale problems. We also explored the application of this method to real-world problems and successfully calibrated a machine learning model to predict the probability of patients developing sepsis. Our results show that this method can be used to improve the calibration of machine learning models in real-world scenarios. Open-world problems present a significant challenge for reinforcement learning, as the agent must adapt to an ever-changing environment with unforeseen tasks and dynamics. In such scenarios, reinforcement learning agents often struggle with the following issues: (1) discovering new tasks, (2) adapting to task changes, and (3) balancing exploration and exploitation in a dynamic task space. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework called Meta Open-World Reinforcement Learning (Meta-OWRL), which utilizes meta-reinforcement learning to develop an agent capable of efficiently exploring and adapting to new tasks. By leveraging a task discovery mechanism and a dynamic task memory, the Meta-OWRL agent can prioritize exploration of previously unencountered tasks, adapt to changes in known tasks, and balance exploration and exploitation. Through extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world robotic platforms, we demonstrate that our proposed Meta-OWRL framework significantly outperforms baseline methods in terms of open-world performance. Furthermore, we showcase the Meta-OWRL agent's ability to generalize to new tasks and adapt to changes in tasks after meta-training. The code and dataset for this work are available at https://github.com/chenyiyong/Meta-OWRL.

This article provides an in-depth examination of the Content Addressable Parallel Processor System (CAPPSS), a cutting-edge technology that utilizes a content-addressable memory (CAM) to perform parallel searches across a vast amount of data. We delve into the fundamental principles of CAPPSS, comprising its core components, including the content-addressable memory unit, priority encoders, decoders, and shift registers. Furthermore, we outline the distinct characteristics of CAPPSS that set it apart from conventional CAMs, such as its ability to execute parallel searches, simultaneous writes, and priority-based operations. Additionally, we explore various applications of CAPPSS in diverse fields like signal processing, machine learning, and database systems. Lastly, we discuss the potential integration of CAPPSS with artificial neural networks and present a design for a hybrid CAPPSS-based neural network. This design is then utilized to develop a pattern recognition system that can handle large datasets. We also present a case study involving the use of CAPPSS for a real-world problem, specifically the identification of malicious network traffic. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of CAPPSS in achieving high accuracy rates with minimal computational overhead. We also examine the design alternatives for CAPPSS and present a performance comparison of different implementations. This comparison highlights the benefits of using CAPPSS over traditional CAMs in terms of speed and energy efficiency. We also discuss the challenges and limitations of CAPPSS, including its scalability and programming complexities. Lastly, we outline the potential future directions for CAPPSS, including its integration with emerging technologies like quantum computing and neuromorphic chips. This raises concerns about the privacy of sensitive information, as a device's password serves as a gateway to its entire contents. This issue is particularly relevant in the context of modern devices, where a single password can reveal extensive amounts of personal data. We develop a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for solving a specific type of constraint satisfaction problem (CSP), namely the minimum sum problem with linear constraints and nonnegative variables. This PTAS solution utilizes a local search approach with an extended neighborhood system, and our method involves a problem-specific parameter determination through an iterative bicriteria shortest path problem solution. Notably, our PTAS is particularly efficient, with each iteration performed in polynomial time. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of at least NP-oracle hardness for CSPs with linear constraints and nonnegative variables, demonstrating that our PTAS achieves a significant improvement over previous approximation algorithms while being close to the theoretical limit for approximate solvability. Additionally, we provide a generalization of our PTAS for CSPs with general integer constraints, and our method is applicable to various optimization problems, including flow problems and multi-commodity cut problems. Several numerical examples and case studies are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of our PTAS. These examples include minimum sum problems, flow problems, multi-commodity cut problems, and a problem in supply chain management. Our results demonstrate the potential of local search-based PTAS for solving a wide range of CSPs with complex constraints. 

Keywords: Polynomial-time approximation scheme, local search, constraint satisfaction problems, minimum sum problem, flow problems, multi-commodity cut problems, supply chain management.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various tasks and are now extensively used in critical areas such as healthcare, finance, and transportation. Given their substantial impact on human life and the economy, it is essential to develop transparent and understandable DNNs. This study focuses on the interpretability of DNNs through Adversarial Training (AT), with the aim of discovering the most relevant features contributing to their predictions. We introduce a novel method, Feature Importance through AT (FIAT), which leverages AT to identify the most influential input features for each prediction class. In contrast to existing methods, FIAT is a class-specific feature importance technique that can handle high-dimensional data and provides a clear, localized understanding of each prediction class. We demonstrate the efficacy of FIAT through comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its superiority over existing methods. Furthermore, FIAT successfully uncovers the underlying patterns in data, revealing the feature importance for each class and enabling the detection of class-specific features. This research is particularly relevant to applications involving human lives, where the transparency of DNNs is crucial for ensuring public trust. Graph neural networks have gained popularity in modeling intricate systems composed of interconnected components, with applications in various fields such as biology, finance, and transportation. By leveraging their ability to handle relational data, GNNs have excelled in tasks including classification, clustering, and link prediction. Despite their success, training GNNs is a complex task due to the challenge of effectively propagating information across the graph structure. This challenge is exacerbated by the presence of noisy or uninformative data within the graph. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework called the Relational Information Propagation Framework (RIP-Framework), which provides a theoretical foundation for analyzing how information is exchanged between nodes in a graph. By breaking down the information exchange process into three components - message passing, aggregation, and update - the RIP-Framework enables the identification of critical factors that influence the quality of information. We demonstrate that the RIP-Framework can be applied to develop robust GNNs capable of resisting the impact of noisy data. Through extensive experiments, we show that these methods achieve superior performance compared to existing techniques on multiple datasets. The code for the proposed methods is available at https://github.com/chen308/rip_framework.

This paper introduces a novel approach to coordinating multiple astrobots tasked with tracking a group of celestial targets across the sky. Unlike previous methods that focus on individual target-astrobot pairs, our approach groups targets by their spectral properties and assigns each astrobot a specific subset to observe. We then develop a discrete optimization problem to schedule astrobots' observations to maximize their overall effectiveness. The problem is NP-hard, so we create a local search algorithm to find near-optimal solutions. Our results show that this algorithm significantly outperforms a random assignment method, and we also examine how the astrobots' coordination is affected by their initial positions and target assignments. Interestingly, our findings indicate that assigning astrobots to observe a specific target or spectral type does not necessarily impact performance, and we propose a simple strategy to achieve optimal results. Finally, we demonstrate the practicality of our approach using real astrobot and telescope data. Our code is available online for other researchers to utilize and adapt for their own projects.

This research addresses the challenge of selecting the best model from a set of sparse models when dealing with categorical variables. This method leverages an innovative distance metric that captures the differences in underlying probability distributions, allowing for the ranking of models based on their similarity to observed data patterns. By utilizing this approach, researchers and data analysts can effectively compare and select the best sparse models, even in complex high-dimensional settings. This study proposes a novel approach to panoramic image stitching that prioritizes vertical alignment.  By analyzing the rotation matrix in the spherical coordinate system, we derive an axis-aligned parameterization that facilitates direct calculation of parallax, ultimately leading to a linear solution for stitching.  Our approach is robust to parallax and barrel distortion, and has been implemented in a user-friendly GUI.  Comparative experiments with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate our vertical alignment approach yields superior results.  Notably, our method's accuracy is significantly less affected by camera misalignment, with a 30 degree error in vertical alignment resulting in only 1.5% error pixels, compared to 10.4% with traditional methods.  Our results also show that vertical alignment can tolerate up to 70 degree error with only 5.4% error pixels.  Furthermore, our method successfully stitches images with significant parallax, including those with notable features and complex backgrounds. The proposed method has the potential to be used in conjunction with MRS imaging to monitor the progression of Parkinson's disease and the effectiveness of treatment. A long sequence modeling technique called dual-path RNNs has been successful in speech separation tasks, but it's limited by high computational requirements and memory usage. To address this issue, we propose a new method called the dual-path convolutional network (DCN) that achieves comparable performance to dual-path RNNs while significantly reducing parameters and requiring less training data. The DCN model leverages the flexibility of convolutional layers to model long sequences and combines this with a time-domain modeling component. Our experiments show that the DCN model outperforms the Conv-TasNet baseline and achieves comparable performance to dual-path RNNs with a substantial reduction in parameters. Notably, the 128-band STFT mask of the DCN model with 256 ms frame length and 128 frequency bins requires only 0.15 million parameters, a 12 times reduction compared to dual-path RNNs. Moreover, the DCN model exhibits robust performance on reverberation time $T_60$ from 0.4s to 0.8s. The code is available at https://github.com/chen308/speech-separation/tree/master/dual-path-convolutional-network.

Experimental results show that RMDN outperforms baseline models in both persona preservation and safety adherence, as evaluated by both automatic metrics and human assessments. Farmers rely on data-driven methods to choose the most effective pesticide treatments, but a major obstacle lies in accurately assessing the efficacy of these treatments using existing statistical methods. A key issue is that the data collected from field trials is contaminated with random errors, which distorts the efficacy estimates and leads to inconsistent rankings of treatment performances. To address this challenge, a new approach is proposed that leverages the concept of robust loss functions to provide a reliable ranking of pesticide treatments by minimizing the impact of measurement errors. A key finding shows that this method yields a consistent and efficient estimator when applied to a specific scenario, and a computational algorithm is developed to accommodate a broader context. Through simulations and real-world applications, the proposed method is compared to alternative strategies, revealing its superiority in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The results demonstrate that the new approach outperforms existing methods in the presence of measurement errors, and a case study involving data from the Fertilizer Experiment Station in Mississippi, USA, illustrates its practical effectiveness. The proposed method has been implemented in the R package called "RobustEfficacy" and is available for public use.

Knowledge distillation is a well-known method that enables the transfer of deep neural network knowledge, where a robust teacher network trains a less complex student network. This technique has shown significant success in model compression and resource allocation. In this research, we propose a novel framework that utilizes knowledge distillation to enhance image recognition by leveraging unlabeled data. By formulating the problem as a distribution matching task, we establish a framework that utilizes correntropy loss to measure the similarity between distributions. We further develop a progressive distillation approach to achieve this goal, where the robust teacher network and the target data distribution are learned simultaneously. The framework is then applied to a color constancy problem, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in a real-world scenario. Experimental results on the Outdoor and Indoor datasets show that our progressive distillation framework outperforms the baseline method, achieving a higher accuracy rate. Moreover, our approach exhibits robustness in scenarios with limited training data. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/Progressive-Distillation.

We introduce a novel imitation learning approach that leverages suboptimal or task-agnostic trajectories in a flexible manner. This method allows us to effectively utilize unlabeled data by learning a latent reward function that guides policy improvement. By doing so, we establish a connection to the problem of discovering reward functions from unsupervised experiences. Our framework's key benefit is its ability to handle suboptimal or task-agnostic trajectories without requiring task-specific data. Notably, our approach outperforms existing imitation learning methods and provides a feasible solution to the challenging problem of discovering reward functions from unsupervised experiences. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method through successful applications in both simulation and real-world experiments. These experiments involve a complex robotic manipulation task and a real-world autonomous driving task, showcasing the potential of our approach to tackle complex problems. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. By imitating optimal policies, agents can bypass suboptimal trial-and-error exploration. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical due to their high cost or unavailability. In contrast, cheaper, noisy feedback is more accessible in many real-world applications. In this paper, we investigate the potential of using noisy feedback to train an imitating agent. We propose a novel framework called "noise-aware imitation learning" that models the relationship between noisy observations and optimal expert behavior. By establishing a connection to the maximum likelihood estimation problem, we develop a robust algorithm to estimate the underlying expert policy. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in scenarios involving noisy feedback. Experimental results using real-world data demonstrate that our system achieves comparable precision to traditional methods using fiducial markers, with a mean absolute error of 3.5 mm for single-view calibration and 2.5 mm for multi-view calibration. Notably, our system outperforms the baseline outlier-prone model by 1.5 mm in single-view and 1 mm in multi-view calibration. The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces has led to the discovery of a non-equilibrium steady state that can be described by a Markovian diagonal matrix, known as the quasi-equilibrium state. This state is reached after a certain number of driving cycles and is characterized by periodic fluctuations that align with the driving forces. In this study, we demonstrate that in systems with random interactions and quenched disorder in their parameters, the quasi-equilibrium state can persist for an exponentially long time, specifically in systems that exhibit localization or ergodic behavior in their ground states. This finding is supported by a theoretical framework that utilizes the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model to show that the duration of this quasi-equilibrium state is directly related to the localization length of the system's eigenstates. This localization length is further demonstrated to be equivalent to the number of driving cycles required for the system to reach its quasi-equilibrium state. This discovery is experimentally confirmed using a photonic quantum simulation. We examine the geometry of a biharmonic hypersurface in a higher-dimensional space, focusing particularly on the properties of recurrent curvature operators in its geometry. We establish several inequalities and identities for the biharmonic hypersurface, and these results lead to a definition of quasi-Einstein property for biharmonic hypersurfaces. We also investigate the relationship between this property and the recurrence of its curvature operators, obtaining a condition that ensures the quasi-Einstein property for biharmonic hypersurfaces in a certain scenario. Additionally, we provide an example to illustrate that a biharmonic hypersurface can exhibit quasi-Einstein behavior without being minimal. Furthermore, we derive a condition for its quasi-Einstein property to be equivalent to being minimal. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for a specific type of biharmonic hypersurface.

We define a rational number p/q and examine the set of words formed from digits 0 through p-1 in the expanded form of nonnegative integers in base p/q. This set is shown to be a regular language using finite automata in (p/q)*10^(p/q-1). A simpler construction is also provided for (p/q)*10^(p/q-1), and this construction is used to create a finite automaton for the quotient field Q_p^x, where x is not equal to 0. This automaton has (p^2-1)(q^2-1)/4 states in (p/q)*10^(p/q-1). Additionally, we present a more complex construction for (p/q)*1, resulting in (p-1)(q-1) states, and discuss potential applications to the study of rational iterated function systems. Lastly, we explore the possibility of extending these constructions to higher-dimensional systems.

u$MSM model, focusing on the impact of new physics at the Giga-Electron-Volt scale.
To resolve this anomaly, we propose the existence of a light, nearly massless
vector boson, the $X$-boson, with a specific interaction with muons.
To explore the $a$Anomaly, we employ a multi-step approach:
first, we determine the required $X$-boson properties to fit the anomaly data;
second, we investigate the production and properties of the $X$-boson in muon colliders,
considering various production channels and decay modes;
third, we examine the $X$-boson's potential to explain the muon magnetic moment anomaly.
Our findings indicate that a muon collider with an energy of 1.5 TeV and 3 ab$^{-1}$ of luminosity at each energy point is the most suitable setup for discovering the $X$-boson through direct production, with an expected significance of 4.5$\sigma$.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $X$-boson can resolve the muon magnetic moment anomaly with a precision of 0.1 ppm. Additionally, we propose the $a$Anomaly to be a potential dark matter candidate, produced through the direct annihilation of the $X$-boson or through the realisation of the Weinberg operator mediated by a scalar or vector field. In this context, we establish the necessary conditions for the $a$Anomaly to be consistent with the observed dark matter density. Finally, we outline the prospects for the $a$Anomaly to be probed at future experiments, including the muon $g-2$ experiment at J-PARC, the COMET neutrino experiment, and the future generation of muon colliders.

By representing flight routes as continuous paths rather than discrete steps, we can optimize performance by minimizing control adjustments along the way. However, this method is computationally expensive, so we've developed a simplified algorithm that uses a limited search area to find the optimal solution quickly. Overall, this method provides a robust solution for continuous shortest path problems, and we're confident that it can be adapted for use in other applications. Emittance scans, a technique used to measure complex final states at colliders, involve varying beam conditions to study their impact on luminosity and background levels. This approach is also found to be robust against potential beam issues and can be combined with other methods to further improve the detection sensitivity. This sequential funding model leads to a first-come-first-served distribution of returns, where those who join earliest have the best chance of receiving a positive return, while those who join later are more likely to lose money. The impact of disasters such as earthquakes on infrastructure and human life is significant, and their consequences are compounded by the limited time available for emergency response and recovery. Social media has emerged as a vital tool in recent years to enhance disaster management and public relations, by facilitating the rapid dissemination of critical information among authorities, relief teams, and the public. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the role of social media in managing earthquake-related events, including the spread of misinformation that can be detrimental to relief efforts. We also discuss the advantages of using machine learning to identify and counter such misinformation, and highlight the importance of developing a real-time, multi-language detection system to effectively tackle this issue. This system would be particularly beneficial in regions with limited resources, where the ability to respond quickly to emerging situations is crucial. To achieve this, we propose a framework that leverages a combination of machine learning techniques, including natural language processing and deep learning, to create a scalable and adaptable system for detecting misinformation on social media platforms. This framework is designed to be applicable to various languages, and its performance can be evaluated using a dataset of labeled tweets. We also present a case study of this framework in the context of earthquake-related events in Turkey, and discuss the challenges and opportunities for further development. This work has the potential to contribute positively to disaster management and public relations efforts in countries with limited resources, and can be adapted for use in other crisis situations. This research is ongoing, and we invite interested parties to collaborate and contribute to this project. Unlike previous methods that focus on 2D image synthesis, our approach leverages 3D transformation learning to expand a basic point cloud model, incorporating real-world rotation, translation, and stretching transformations. To achieve this, we employ a two-stage framework consisting of a semantic-aware transformation module and a transformation expansion module. This framework is trained end-to-end using a synthetic dataset, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Notably, our approach outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and diversity, as evidenced by generated point clouds and mesh models. Moreover, we successfully apply our method to real-world scenarios, including generating point clouds from 2D drawings and creating 3D models from written descriptions. The code and models are available at https://github.com/zheng0625/text2pointcloud.

In frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar networks, carrier sense multiple access (CSMA) is a suitable medium access control (MAC) protocol due to its simplicity and effectiveness. However, the performance of traditional CSMA is hindered by the limited knowledge of radar signal characteristics, such as the modulation function and sampling rate. In this paper, we investigate the optimal clear channel assessment (CCA) function for CSMA protocols in FMCW radar networks. By analyzing the characteristics of radar signals, we propose a novel CCA function based on the similarity between received waveforms. This allows for the identification of co-sensing radars and the estimation of interference. Furthermore, we develop a distributed algorithm for optimal CCA function learning and demonstrate its convergence and optimality. Simulations validate the proposed approach, revealing its superior performance in comparison to random CCA functions. Additionally, we investigate the impact of CCA function complexity on network performance. Notably, we observe that the optimal CCA function can be highly complex, but a simplified variant achieves near-optimal results. This finding highlights the significance of balancing CCA complexity and performance in practical applications. Through this research, we provide a foundation for optimizing CSMA protocols in heterogeneous wireless sensor networks, enabling coexistence between radar and other wireless systems. This work has the potential to be extended to other types of heterogeneous wireless systems, such as those involving magnetic sensors and radar systems. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Recent studies have successfully applied this approach to various domains,
including biomedical and finance. However, existing methods primarily focus
on event-based temporal relation and often overlook the temporal information
embedded in event timestamps. This study introduces a novel approach that
incorporates a temporal knowledge graph completion framework, leveraging both
event-based temporal relations and timestamp information. We enhance the
conventional TransE by adding a temporal relation pattern learning module and
a temporal relation prediction module. This approach is further extended to
temporal relation pattern learning for graph inference. Experimental results on
both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our
proposed method. Moreover, we apply this approach to a real-world case study
in the biomedical domain, successfully inferring missing event information
for the COVID-19 vaccine development knowledge graph. Our code is available at
https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/temporal-knowledge-graph-completion.

Recent studies on the giant resonance in $^{16}$O's electric dipole excitations have found that it doesn't exist as a single entity but rather as a combination of multiple resonances with distinct characteristics. Using the RPA-SDarT approach, we successfully reconstituted the $^{16}$O electric dipole strength function from experimental data and found it to be composed of three main resonance components: the well-known 3.53 MeV $\rm{1^{-}}$ state, a previously unreported resonance at 10.4 MeV with a $\rm{1^{-}}$ configuration, and a broad, low-energy resonance at around 6-8 MeV with mixed $\rm{1^{-}}$ and $\rm{3^{-}}$ configurations. We also found that the low-energy resonance is a result of the breakdown of the harmonic oscillator shell model and is caused by the coupling between the $s$-shell and the $p$-shell, which leads to the mixing of $\rm{1^{-}}$ and $\rm{3^{-}}$ configurations. Furthermore, we found that the 3.53 MeV $\rm{1^{-}}$ state and the 10.4 MeV $\rm{1^{-}}$ state have distinct characteristics, with the former being a resonance with a large neutron-proton pair correlation and the latter being a resonance with a large neutron correlation. We also found that the 10.4 MeV $\rm{1^{-}}$ state has a large neutron correlation and a large energy gap between the filled and the unfilled orbitals, which makes it a good candidate for a quasiparticle state. Clustering is a fundamental concept in data analysis that has been extensively studied and applied across various disciplines. The development of effective clustering methods is crucial, especially in the big data era. Many real-world systems, including social networks, evolve dynamically over time, with applications such as Twitter and Reddit. These changes can be rapid and unpredictable, rendering traditional clustering methods that focus on static data less effective. In this paper, we present a novel approach called Dynamic Community Discovery (DCD) that leverages incremental clustering and utilizes historical data to inform and refine its results. DCD is an adaptable framework that can be integrated with existing community discovery algorithms to detect dynamic communities. We demonstrate the efficacy of DCD through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, including Twitter and Reddit, and show that it outperforms traditional methods. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/DCD.

Deep Neural Text Generation Models (DNTGs) have achieved remarkable success in the past decade, with numerous breakthroughs in various applications. Among these models, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have proven particularly effective. However, training GANs is notoriously difficult due to the difficulty in balancing the generator updates. This challenge is exacerbated by the need to train a discriminator that is both effective in distinguishing real and generated data and preventing mode dropping. To address this issue, a novel training method called balanced generator and discriminator updates is proposed. This approach involves training the generator and discriminator in an alternating manner with a focus on balancing the loss functions. The proposed method is versatile and can be integrated with existing GAN architectures. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach leads to significant improvements in text generation tasks, including language translation, summarization, and conversation. The concept of interstellar panspermia posits that life can be transferred between star systems, either through comets or other celestial bodies. While this idea is difficult to verify through direct observation, we can test it by examining the conditions necessary for life to survive during transport. In this study, we analyze the likelihood of microorganisms surviving the transition from a planetary system to another, using the example of the journey from the Alpha Centauri system to the nearby system of TRAPPIST-1. By considering various factors, such as the velocity of Oort Cloud comets and the time it takes for them to reach other star systems, we estimate that it would take around 1-10 million years for comets to travel from Alpha Centauri to TRAPPIST-1. However, during this time, comets would experience significant changes due to radiation and the effects of stellar flares from both Alpha Centauri and TRAPPIST-1. As a result, the chances of life surviving this journey are relatively low, around 1-10%. Notably, the presence of a stable habitable world like Earth, with a robust biosphere and internal heat, would greatly enhance the chances of life surviving this transition. In contrast, microorganisms on comets or other small bodies would face a much higher risk of extinction during this journey. Ultimately, this study suggests that interstellar panspermia may be feasible, but it would likely be limited to life forms that can withstand the harsh conditions of space and survive for extended periods of time. In the case of the Alpha Centauri system, we propose that the habitable zone might be contaminated with life from other star systems, potentially making it more likely to detect biosignatures there. In contrast, the TRAPPIST-1 system, with its seven Earth-sized planets, may be more likely to harbor life that originated from comets carrying microorganisms from the Alpha Centauri system. Understanding how animals utilize space and select resources is crucial for effective wildlife management. This knowledge can be obtained through resource selection functions (RSFs), which estimate the probability of animal occurrence based on environmental factors. Our study employed RSFs to investigate the habitat preferences of female white-tailed deer in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan during the fall season. We analyzed data from 2015 to 2019, collected through radio-telemetry of 104 females, and identified their home ranges within the Marquette and Alger counties. Using spatially explicit models, we found that deer preferred areas with higher cover of deciduous trees, particularly oak and maple, and avoided areas with coniferous cover and near roads. These findings suggest that maintaining deciduous vegetation and minimizing road construction in deer habitats could be beneficial for conservation and management. Additionally, we developed a habitat suitability index to predict deer occurrence at a local scale, which can be applied in the future to estimate population sizes. This study contributes to the existing literature on deer ecology and provides a framework for using RSFs to inform habitat management decisions. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of this method to other deer species and habitats. Our approach can be adapted for use with other wildlife species and habitats, and we highlight the importance of integrating RSFs with population models to make informed management decisions. Lastly, we emphasize the value of incorporating citizen science data into future studies. This research can serve as a model for other studies examining the habitat preferences of wildlife species. Evaluating a football team's defensive capabilities is a complex task, as it depends on multiple variables including the opponent's attacking strength and the specific game conditions. Past research has attempted to assess defense using general metrics such as goals conceded, but these methods fail to account for the unique circumstances of each match. In contrast, our proposed approach utilizes machine learning to develop a comprehensive, context-aware evaluation of defense, taking into consideration factors including the opponent's attacking power, the score difference, home advantage, and weather conditions. By training and testing this model on historical Premier League data, we demonstrate its ability to accurately predict the likelihood of conceding goals in various defensive situations. Furthermore, we utilize this framework to identify key defensive strengths and weaknesses for each team during the 2019-2020 season, providing insights that can inform coaching strategies and team management. By considering the nuances of each match situation, our approach offers a more refined and detailed assessment of football team defense than existing methods. Through this work, we contribute a new, context-aware framework for evaluating football team defense, along with a comprehensive analysis of the defensive strategies employed by Premier League teams during the 2019-2020 season. Extracting information from historical forms is a labor-intensive task, where the lack of clear guidelines and standardized formats poses significant challenges. This study focuses on automatically extracting information from French forms created between 1871 and 1940, which were previously inaccessible due to their deteriorated condition. We introduce a novel approach, combining pre-trained vision and language models to address this problem. First, we utilize a pre-trained text-to-image model to generate synthetic images of forms, which are then used to train a form understanding model. This model is then fine-tuned on real images of forms. Our approach demonstrates the potential for extracting information from historical forms with deteriorated images, and our results show that it outperforms a baseline model trained solely on real images. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/alexmdev/extracting-info-from-historical-forms. Our findings were presented at the 2023 IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops.

Real-world time series data is often dynamic, containing multiple interconnected components that evolve over time, making it challenging for a single model to capture their dynamics. While Recurrent State-space models (RSSMs) have demonstrated flexibility and performance in modeling such data, they can be difficult to train and typically require a large number of parameters. In response to these challenges, we propose a novel multi-component state-space model called the Hierarchical RSSM (H-RSSM), which utilizes a hierarchical latent space to capture multiple factors within a single time series. By leveraging the structure of the hierarchical model, we develop an efficient learning algorithm that significantly reduces training time and memory usage. Evaluations on multiple real-world datasets have shown that H-RSSM outperforms RSSM and other competitive baselines in terms of prediction accuracy and model compactness. Moreover, H-RSSM exhibits superior performance in modeling complex temporal dynamics and identifying key factors that influence these dynamics. Additionally, we demonstrate the interpretability of H-RSSM by successfully applying it to analyze the dynamics of a real-world dataset. The code for H-RSSM is available at https://github.com/tingyf/h-rssm.

The problem of estimating polarization in social systems has been extensively studied, yet the issue of selecting the optimal method remains unresolved. This study proposes a novel framework for evaluating and comparing polarization measurement methods. By applying these methods to real-world data from Reddit, we assess the impact of methodological choices on results and find that some methods yield similar findings, while others produce distinct outcomes. We introduce HyperPrompt, a novel framework that leverages hypernetworks to generate task-specific prompts for language models like BERT and RoBERTa. By utilizing a parameter-efficient prompt generation approach, HyperPrompt enables automatic creation of prompts that adapt to particular tasks and produce high-quality results. Unlike previous methods that rely on manual design or require additional training, HyperPrompt develops a hypernetwork to create prompts dynamically. This approach leads to a significant reduction in additional parameters compared to direct parameter learning. Our experiments demonstrate that HyperPrompt achieves superior performance on diverse NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, question answering, and paraphrasing, by producing high-quality prompts that effectively guide the underlying language models. Notably, HyperPrompt outperforms strong baselines, such as Prefix-Tuning and AnnBERT, by a substantial margin of 4.5% in accuracy on the QALM dataset. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the generated prompts exhibit semantic similarity to human-provided labels and effectively map task-specific features from the input to the output. Furthermore, we observe that HyperPrompt excels in low-resource settings and achieves a notable 10.5% improvement in accuracy on the SQuAD dataset with only 100 labeled samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-CLAPA/HyperPrompt.

This paper introduces a novel knowledge distillation framework that enables the transfer of ranking knowledge from a high-performance teacher model to multiple student models simultaneously. The key insight is that the teacher model's predictions can be treated as reliable ranking orders, which are then used to guide the learning of student models through pairwise comparison. A key challenge arises from the large number of pairwise constraints generated, which significantly hinders optimization efficiency. To address this issue, we propose a dynamic sampling approach to selectively focus on the most informative comparisons. By doing so, we significantly reduce the sampling time while maintaining substantial gains in performance. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework, achieving notable improvements of up to 10.4% in NDCG@10 compared to naive distillation methods. Moreover, our approach is computationally efficient, delivering comparable performance to single-teacher distillation with only a 1.35 times increase in sampling time. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-wang/ranking-kd.

This study extends linear gyrokinetic theory to investigate geodesic acoustic modes (GAMs) in ion temperature anisotropy, and applies this to a tokamak equilibrium with a linear density gradient. By solving the linearized gyrokinetic Hamiltonian equation using a new variable transformation, we derive a linearized drift-kinetic equation that considers ion temperature anisotropy effects. The equation is then solved to obtain the dispersion relation of GAMs, revealing that ion temperature anisotropy increases the frequency of modes with resonant frequencies closer to the geodesic frequency, and has a stabilizing effect on modes with frequencies far from the geodesic frequency. Notably, the anisotropy also leads to the excitation of a higher frequency mode, referred to as the geodesic acoustic wave mode (GAWM), with a frequency approximately twice that of the GAM. The growth rate of both modes is found to be low, with the GAWM exhibiting a weaker growth rate than the GAM. The frequency and growth rate of these modes are found to be robust against variations in ion temperature anisotropy and magnetic shear. Advanced composite materials composed of fibers embedded in an electrically conductive matrix possess exceptional mechanical strength and unique detectability properties. A novel inverse method is presented, utilizing an electrical impedance tomography (EIT) technique to map conductivity variations within the damaged area. A finite element method (FEM) is employed to create a forward solver, while a level set method (LSM) is utilized to constrain and refine potential damage areas. The algorithm iteratively updates and refines these areas to minimize the difference between simulated and actual impedance data. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in identifying and quantifying damage in both linear and nonlinear cases. Additionally, the method is validated through physical testing on a real-world application, involving the detection of debonding in a carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) patch bonded to aluminum. Results from this experiment show that the proposed algorithm successfully detects and quantifies the extent of debonding. This study provides a comprehensive framework for non-invasive, real-time monitoring of damage within composite materials through changes in their electrical conductivity. Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have shown promise in using neural signals to restore mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. While BCIs have successfully helped people walk again, these systems are often limited to short periods of support due to their reliance on motor cortex signals, which can degrade over time. An alternative approach focuses on the brain's sensory feedback systems, which remain intact even in severe spinal cord injuries. This concept posits that by restoring sensory feedback to the brain, it can relearn how to control walking without the need for direct motor cortex stimulation. This review explores existing research on sensory BCIs for walking restoration, including the neural mechanisms involved and potential targets for BCI interventions. It also discusses the challenges and potential solutions for developing reliable and long-lasting sensory BCIs, which could provide sustained support for walking in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Furthermore, it outlines potential future directions for this area of research. By examining the current state of sensory BCIs for walking restoration, this review aims to inspire new ideas and approaches to overcome the technical hurdles and unlock the full potential of these systems. We establish that a right-angled Artin group with a non-finite, minimal action on a tree that is not a line has an infinite number of unbounded branches in its graph. This conclusion generalizes previous findings of Minematsu and Fujiwara. Additionally, we provide a characterization for right-angled Artin groups with finite, minimal actions on trees that are not lines, involving the absence of specific graph components. Furthermore, we present a right-angled Artin group whose action on a tree that is not a line has a finite, minimal period. We also derive a condition for right-angled Artin groups to have finite, minimal actions on trees that are not lines, involving the absence of certain graph components and the finiteness of a specific parameter. This condition is utilized to construct an infinite family of right-angled Artin groups with finite, minimal actions on trees that are not lines, for any given positive integer. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between the structure of right-angled Artin groups and their actions on trees that are not lines, and we provide a question regarding this relationship.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a comprehensive framework for modeling the evolutionary histories of species by incorporating reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more accurate representation of the complex evolutionary processes that have shaped the evolution of species and their genomes. This tutorial will delve into the fundamental concepts of phylogenetic networks, focusing on their construction from multiple phylogenetic trees and the underlying mathematical principles that govern them. Building on this foundation, we will explore various computational methods for building phylogenetic networks, including those that utilize multiple alignments of sequences and those that incorporate additional data types, such as genomic rearrangements and gene family evolution. Through a series of case studies, we will demonstrate the application of phylogenetic networks to analyze the evolution of various organisms and genome structures, including prokaryotes, eukaryotes, and human populations. By highlighting the benefits and limitations of phylogenetic networks, we aim to encourage researchers to utilize these networks as a valuable tool for exploring the complex evolutionary histories of species and their genomes. This tutorial is designed for researchers with a basic understanding of phylogenetics and computational biology, and it is suitable for both established researchers and graduate students in the field. We investigate a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with randomly varying on-site potential fluctuations, drawing from different distribution types. This model exhibits a topological Anderson insulating phase when the disorder is weak, and we find that it can be described by the Zak phase and Bose-Einstein condensate correlation function. Notably, this phase can also be understood through the localization of edge states and by analyzing the Fermi winding number in the presence of disorder. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phase can be characterized by the emergence of a gap in the Bose-Einstein condensate correlation function at the Fermi level in the disorder average, and this phase is distinguished from the topological Anderson phase by the presence of chiral edge states in the latter. Our findings are relevant to the interpretation of experimental data from superconducting qubit arrays.

This research develops a new statistical test for linearity in continuous-time diffusion models, extending previous work by Huang and Kostomarov (2020) which was limited to models with observable drift components. The proposed test, referred to as the quasi-score linearity test, can be applied to models where the drift function is not directly observable. We introduce a novel framework called deep declarative networks, which represents a wide range of optimization-based models, including those with moving objectives and constraints. This framework enables the computation of exact gradients for model predictions, leveraging the properties of specific models. By drawing parallels with the concept of implicit functions, we demonstrate that differentiating the solutions to parametrized optimization problems essentially amounts to solving a specific optimization problem. This understanding allows us to derive an efficient algorithm for computing exact gradients, which can be applied to a broad class of optimization-based models, including those involving moving constraints and objectives. This includes the ability to compute exact gradients for models such as shifting least squares, moving linear programs, and dynamic constraint learning. We showcase the effectiveness of this approach through experiments in implicit models, dynamic constraint learning, and time-series prediction. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/tingyf/ddn.

The rise of cryptocurrency through mining and transaction fees has led to significant investments in blockchain technology, with some platforms now rivaling established banking systems in size and usage. As a result, cybercriminals are increasingly targeting these blockchain platforms with sophisticated malware designed to exploit vulnerabilities and deceive users. To combat this threat, law enforcement agencies and cybersecurity experts require a deeper understanding of the evolution of blockchain-based malware, its spread, and the illicit activities it enables. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of various types of blockchain-based malware, including their operational mechanisms, the vulnerabilities they target, and the programming languages used to develop them. By examining 15 distinct malware variants, we reveal the common tactics employed by cybercriminals to exploit blockchain platforms and the unique challenges they face in spreading malware across multiple wallets. Our findings highlight the importance of improving wallet security, enhancing blockchain platform security, and developing more effective cybersecurity measures to prevent the spread of malware. Additionally, we outline potential research directions for identifying and mitigating the risks associated with blockchain-based malware. By shedding light on this critical issue, we aim to raise awareness among cybersecurity professionals, researchers, and policymakers about the growing threat of blockchain-based malware and the need for a unified approach to address it. By collaborating and sharing knowledge, we can work towards creating a safer and more secure blockchain ecosystem. This study is an extension of our previous research presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Blockchain and Cryptocurrency, and it includes new insights and analysis of additional malware variants. Topological error-correcting codes, which are highly resilient against random errors, are crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, generating and measuring these codes require multiple steps and involve a high number of quantum operations, potentially hindering their application due to resource constraints. This limitation can be overcome by using a decoding process that identifies and erases faulty quantum gates within the quantum circuit, a process known as gauge-invariant decoding. We present a novel quantum algorithm that accurately determines the location and type of single-qubit Pauli errors in a surface code by applying this decoding approach. By utilizing a sequence of quantum circuits that measure the effect of applying a logical NOT gate on individual physical qubits, we successfully locate and correct errors with high accuracy in both simulations and actual experiments. Notably, this method demonstrates a significant improvement over conventional techniques, achieving a 50% reduction in measurement count required for error correction. Furthermore, our approach can be executed on a faulty quantum computer itself, providing a foundation for developing more complex fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. By combining this method with other techniques, we demonstrate the ability to recover from multiple-qubit Pauli errors and even stabilize unstable states in quantum circuits. Our findings offer a path forward for developing practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

In the context of memoryless contextual linear bandits, we've developed a new algorithm called DMCBL that achieves near-optimal regret performance. By considering a linear contextual model and assuming that context vectors are mutually independent and have a bounded spectral norm, DMCBL's regret performance improves to $\tilde{O}(d^2\cdot\kappa^2\cdot\tau)$ in the fixed context case and $\tilde{O}(d^2\cdot\kappa^2\cdot n^{2d/2}\cdot\tau)$ in the general case, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of action vectors and $n$ represents the number of context vectors. Notably, this yields approximately $2d$ bits of context information per context for the memoryless contextual linear bandit problem, outperforming the best-known previous bound by a significant margin. Moreover, DMCBL's performance in the dynamic context case is comparable to the best-known previous bound, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments. By leveraging a novel low-rank matrix estimation technique, DMCBL's performance is substantially improved compared to existing methods. Additionally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(d^2\cdot\kappa^2\cdot\tau)$ for the fixed context case, confirming the tightness of our upper bound. This work provides a novel solution to the distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit problem and offers a new approach to low-rank matrix estimation. We introduce a novel framework for an efficient policy evaluation method called
Retrospective Distribution Learning (RDL). RDL leverages access to data from the
testing distribution during the training stage, enabling the discovery of a proxy
retrospective distribution that closely matches the desired outcome distribution.
By developing a precise evaluation protocol and benchmarking RDL on both real
and artificial datasets, our findings demonstrate that our approach outperforms
existing methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Notably, RDL
achieves a significant 2.5x speedup in policy evaluation compared to the
state-of-the-art method, while also delivering a 0.15 in NDCG, a key performance
metric. Moreover, our analysis reveals that RDL's efficiency stems from its
ability to utilize a smaller number of negative samples, amounting to a 4x
reduction, without compromising performance. By exploring the relationship between
the testing and retrospective distributions, we uncover key insights that
facilitate the design of more effective algorithms. Ultimately, our work paves the
way for the development of more efficient and accurate algorithms in the realm
of efficient policy evaluation. The code and data for our experiments are
available at https://github.com/chen308/Retrospective-Distribution-Learning.

This research focuses on resolving the challenge of legged locomotion on deformable terrain, specifically addressing the difficulty of predicting and adapting to the dynamic interactions between the legged robot and the terrain. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages a physics-based simulation framework to model the dynamic behavior of the terrain and the legged robot. This framework is integrated with a learning-based control system that utilizes reinforcement learning to optimize terrain-aware control policies. To train these policies efficiently, we employ a multi-fidelity learning strategy that leverages both high-fidelity simulation-based rollouts and low-fidelity simulation-based rollouts. The proposed approach is validated through simulations and physical experiments on a humanoid robot, demonstrating its effectiveness in adapting to various types of deformable terrain. The results show that the proposed method can achieve significant performance improvements over traditional control methods, particularly in terms of stability and speed, and can generalize to new, unseen terrain types. In contrast, our proposed approach, Hierarchical Graph Encoder with Contextualized Attention (HiGEC), utilizes a graph neural network that encodes both node representations and contextualized attention mechanisms to build contextual relationships among nodes, ultimately generating a hierarchical structure that accurately reflects semantic relationships. Our experiments demonstrate that HiGEC outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in both automatic evaluation and human assessment on two widely used datasets, showcasing its ability to create more effective and visually appealing information hierarchies. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the advantages of using contextualized attention mechanisms in graph neural networks, particularly in relation to node degree and graph density. By leveraging HiGEC, both data visualization practitioners and researchers can easily integrate this model into their workflows to create high-quality information hierarchies. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/HierGraphEncoder.

This paper presents a sentiment analysis model that leverages deep learning techniques, utilizing a dataset of tweets and Instagram posts collected from March to May 2020, during the peak of the pandemic in India. Experimental results show that the proposed model, based on a bidirectional long short-term memory network with an attention mechanism and a convolutional neural network, achieves exceptional performance, with accuracy rates of 87.5% and 86.2% for the Twitter and Instagram datasets, respectively. The study also explores the effectiveness of using additional features, such as part-of-speech tags and named entity recognition, which are found to have a limited impact on the sentiment analysis task. The proposed model exhibits robust performance across various evaluation metrics, including F1-score, which is particularly important for this application. The findings of this study can contribute to the development of more effective sentiment analysis models and provide valuable insights for researchers working on related tasks, such as opinion mining and crisis management. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to significant advancements in various applications, including image classification, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. However, research has revealed that machine learning models are susceptible to hidden vulnerabilities, specifically backdoor attacks, which involve creating a covert mechanism that triggers a model to misclassify specific input patterns. These triggers can be embedded in models during training and remain undetected during normal operation. Existing detection methods primarily focus on identifying anomalies in model predictions but are limited by their reliance on labeled data and may not generalize well to real-world scenarios. In this study, we introduce a novel framework that leverages transfer learning and utilizes unlabeled data to detect backdoors. Our approach involves training a detection model on a small labeled dataset and fine-tuning it with a large dataset of unlabeled data, demonstrating improved performance compared to models trained on labeled data alone. Experimental results on corrupted MNIST, CIFAR10, and CelebA datasets show that our framework effectively detects backdoors with high accuracy, even in scenarios with trigger sizes as small as 1 pixel. Notably, our method achieves a significant improvement of over 20% in accuracy when using unlabeled data, outperforming the baseline model that relies on labeled data by a margin of over 40%. Furthermore, our framework exhibits robustness in scenarios with varying trigger sizes, occlusions, and target labels. This research focuses on protecting deep learning inference from inference attacks and overfitting. To achieve this, we propose a novel secure inference framework that incorporates a dual optimization approach. By doing so, we optimize both linear and non-linear layers of pre-trained neural networks to defend against inference attacks and prevent data leakage. Our proposed framework leverages a unique dual formulation that ensures the protection of sensitive information while maintaining high accuracy in inference. Notably, our framework offers significant improvements over existing secure inference methods, outperforming them by a substantial margin of 10.4% in terms of accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Moreover, our framework is highly efficient, capable of processing 10 million inference requests per second on a single GPU. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, showcasing its robustness and scalability. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the knowledge augmentation and fusion techniques used in KARN, which shows that our approach effectively incorporates relevant knowledge and improves the model's performance. Notably, we observe that KARN excels in answering questions that require reasoning over extended time periods and have a higher proportion of unknown words. In the context of a Federated Learning system, where multiple nodes with private data want to collaborate on a shared goal, it's common for data to be unevenly distributed among these nodes. This disparity in data distribution creates a challenge for the learning algorithm, as it typically requires access to a broad range of data samples. A common approach to address this issue is by using a deep neural network with a shared feature extractor and a node-specific classifier for each data source. However, this method has a significant drawback: it can lead to overfitting, as each classifier is trained independently, resulting in suboptimal performance. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new algorithm that enables the learning of a robust feature extractor and a unified classifier for multiple data sources. This is achieved by introducing a new optimization objective that balances the classification error for each node while encouraging the sharing of features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, including the famous CIFAR-10 dataset. The results show that our proposed algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, including the popular FedProx algorithm, by providing a more robust and accurate solution. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of our algorithm under certain conditions. Notably, we demonstrate that our algorithm can tolerate significant heterogeneity in data distribution among nodes, including scenarios where one node has a significantly larger dataset than the others. This is particularly relevant in real-world applications of Federated Learning, where data distribution among nodes can be highly uneven. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the effect of data heterogeneity on the convergence of our algorithm. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the design of Federated Learning algorithms in the presence of data heterogeneity. This research has significant potential to accelerate the development of Federated Learning algorithms that can handle real-world data distributions. This work is part of a larger research project that aims to develop a new class of Federated Learning algorithms capable of tolerating significant data heterogeneity among nodes. This study examines the long-term effects of court-ordered mental health treatment on recidivism among offenders on probation. By leveraging a large dataset from the Florida State Courts, we employ a method that controls for selection bias to analyze the outcomes. Our findings indicate that receiving mental health treatment during probation significantly reduces the likelihood of offenders returning to the criminal justice system within five years, with a notable effect observed in the first two years. Furthermore, the results show that mental health treatment has a more pronounced effect on violent recidivism than non-violent recidivism. To better understand these outcomes, we explore the relationship between mental health treatment and time to recidivism, revealing that treatment delays the onset of recidivism and accelerates the time to first non-violent conviction. These results suggest that mental health treatment has a positive impact on both violent and non-violent offenders, with a potential mechanism being reduced time to first violent conviction. Notably, we discover that the effectiveness of treatment varies by age, with younger offenders experiencing greater benefits than older offenders. Additionally, we uncover a potential issue of treatment duration, with longer treatment periods associated with increased recidivism risk. These findings provide valuable insights for policymakers aiming to optimize the allocation of limited mental health resources within the criminal justice system.

The success of medical image segmentation relies heavily on accurate pixel-level annotation, which remains a time-consuming and resource-intensive process. This study proposes an unsupervised learning approach that enables automatic annotation of medical images using self-supervised segmentation and consistency training. By applying this approach to brain tumor segmentation, our results show improved performance compared to a baseline model without annotation, achieving a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.83 on the BRATS 2015 dataset. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this method can generalize to other medical image segmentation tasks, as evidenced by comparable scores on the CVC Clinics dataset for skin lesion segmentation. The code and models are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangsun/Unsupervised-Consistency-Training-Annotation.
