To validate the performance of this system, a thorough simulation of various QCD and non-QCD processes is necessary. This simulation involves the generation of primary interactions using PYTHIA 6.4, PYTHIA 8, and HERWIG++ 2.3, which are then processed through the CMS detector simulation based on GEANT 4. To assess the jet identification efficiency, a detailed study of the system's response to different generators is required. This study compares the efficiency of the jet identification system for each generator, and the results show that the response varies by 0.1-1.0% for the majority of the generators, with the exception of PYTHIA 6.4, which exhibits a 1-5% discrepancy due to its distinct parton shower and hadronization patterns. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the jet identification system can reduce the systematic uncertainty associated with the measurement of the Higgs boson properties due to the choice of generator from 1-2% to less than 1%. This paper introduces ArtNet, a novel neural rendering framework that utilizes
articulated 3D models for virtual humans, enabling high-quality, real-time
rendering and editing of their appearances and movements. Unlike traditional
methods that rely on per-pixel optimization, ArtNet leverages a compact 3D
representation to capture per-vertex details and adaptability. By combining
both image and 3D data, ArtNet achieves remarkable results, including removing
accessories, occlusions, and editing facial features and hair. Our approach
consists of an articulated neural rendering network that maps images to 3D models,
and a complementary auxiliary network that corrects rendering errors. We
demonstrate ArtNet's capabilities through a range of applications, including
avatar creation, removal, and editing, and achieve state-of-the-art results on
the FaceForeniscs++ benchmark. Our code and models are available at
https://github.com/zh116436/ArtNet. Our video demo can be found at
https://youtu.be/6Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8. Our paper is scheduled for presentation at CVPR 2023.

The long-term functionality and lifespan of materials depend heavily on their resistance to atomic disorder, a common occurrence that can stem from various sources including mechanical stress, chemical reactions, and thermal fluctuations. Understanding the spatial distribution of order and disorder at the atomic level is crucial for predicting a material's performance and potential for failure. In this research, a novel approach is presented that leverages machine learning to classify local atomic environments in crystalline materials as either ordered or disordered. This approach is highly accurate, surpassing traditional methods by a significant margin, especially in areas with complex atomic arrangements. The results show that the learned models effectively capture the subtle differences in local atomic structure, even in regions with minimal symmetry, and are capable of distinguishing between various types of disorder. Furthermore, the models can be applied to any material property that is a function of the local atomic environment, enabling the prediction of order and disorder across different temperatures and compositions. The potential of this approach is demonstrated through the analysis of grain boundary disorder in copper, revealing a more complex structure than previously understood. The research also highlights the potential for this framework to be used in conjunction with other methods to study the dynamics of materials over time. By providing a detailed description of the algorithm and its implementation, this study offers a machine learning solution that can be adapted for the analysis of other materials and phenomena. The code is openly available for the benefit of the materials science community. Through this research, a foundation is laid for the development of machine learning models that can accurately capture the intricate dynamics of local atomic disorder in materials. Knowledge tracing, a predictive model, forecasts students' future knowledge based on their past performance and history of interactions, allowing for personalized learning pathways. Deep knowledge tracing (DKT) is a prominent approach that achieves high accuracy but is limited by its complexity and inability to provide insights into learned features. To address this, we propose a novel, transparent, and interpretable knowledge tracing framework called multi-task factorized knowledge tracing (MTF-KT). This framework simultaneously addresses multiple knowledge tracing tasks while sharing latent factors across all tasks, effectively capturing task-agnostic knowledge representations. By doing so, MTF-KT enables the generation of detailed feature maps that provide a clear understanding of the learned knowledge representations. Our experiments demonstrate that MTF-KT outperforms DKT on multiple datasets and achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art KT models while offering transparent knowledge representations. The generated feature maps also reveal interesting knowledge patterns and enable the identification of key knowledge components for each task. This is further supported by a case study on the mathematics knowledge graph. The code and data are available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-wu/MTF-KT.

This paper introduces a novel approach to adapting Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) models across new domains with only a few examples. Unlike existing methods that rely on explicit feature extraction and domain classification, we propose a meta-learning framework that leverages the shared structure across domains and effectively utilizes the labeled data for each new sample. By employing a parameter-efficient domain-specific conditioner and utilizing a shared GEC model, our framework achieves state-of-the-art results on the CoNLL-2009 task with only a few examples per domain. Notably, our results show that our meta-learning approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art in few-shot GEC, with a significant improvement of +2.34 F-score when adapting to a new domain with just five labeled examples. Moreover, our framework exhibits robust performance in cross-domain evaluation, surpassing the current best score by +1.45 F-score when adapting to a domain with 20 labeled examples. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/zheng062/maml-gec.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. It demonstrates that several prominent databases suffer from this leakage, enabling an unauthorized user to deduce the update history of sensitive data. Furthermore, 'update pattern leakage' is shown to be powerful enough to reveal highly sensitive information, such as the presence of a user's medical history, by simply querying the database with minimal information. To address this issue, we propose an enhanced database 'EncDecGraph', which effectively prevents 'update pattern leakage' through the secure disclosure of update graphs, while maintaining query efficiency via an optimized subgraph matching technique. Our results show that 'EncDecGraph' achieves a significant reduction in query latency, outperforming existing databases by several orders of magnitude. The design and performance of 'EncDecGraph' are thoroughly evaluated through both theoretical and practical assessments, demonstrating its capability to prevent 'update pattern leakage' with minimal latency. The source code for 'EncDecGraph' is available at https://github.com/chenyong77/EncDecGraph.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the capabilities of re-identification models, yet there's still a substantial gap between real-world applications and the limited datasets used to train these models. In contrast to other datasets, surveillance videos typically lack labels and contain a large number of unannotated samples. In this paper, we argue that there's a wealth of valuable information hidden within these unlabeled videos, which can be leveraged to enhance re-identification performance. To achieve this, we introduce a novel framework called Cross-Video Contrastive Learning (CVCL), which utilizes unlabeled videos to learn robust features. Specifically, CVCL incorporates a contrastive learning module to bridge the gap between distinct video appearances of the same person, as well as a hard negative mining module to focus on difficult samples. Through extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets, MSMTL and VehicleID, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, demonstrating the effectiveness of CVCL. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/CVCL.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is a pressing challenge in reinforcement learning, as it must address the issue of how to effectively utilize unrelated data from individual agents that may have significantly different levels of competence. In this research, we introduce a novel offline learning setting called the "Mixed Individual Multi-Agent Setting" (MIMAS), characterized by a group of agents with varying levels of performance working towards a common goal. Unlike existing offline multi-agent settings that assume all agents can achieve optimal results with perfect data, MIMAS requires offline learning to handle data from agents with suboptimal policies. We demonstrate that directly applying offline learning methods from single-agent settings results in unsatisfying team outcomes. To address this issue, we propose a new offline learning approach called "Mixed Individual Multi-Agent Policy Intervention" (MIMAPI), which involves first identifying a set of high-performance trajectories from the data and then developing a team policy that intervenes in the best actions from these trajectories. We show that MIMAPI can achieve optimal team outcomes in MIMAS compared to other offline learning methods. Additionally, we present a practical algorithm for MIMAPI and verify its effectiveness through experiments on various scenarios, including complex gridworld environments and a self-driving scenario. The code for these experiments is available on the corresponding project webpage.

This research addresses the challenge of registering megavoltage images obtained from radiation therapy treatments.  Traditional image registration techniques rely on intensity-based similarity metrics, which are sensitive to radiation artifacts and dark backgrounds often found in megavoltage images.  To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that combines multi-scale feature descriptors and a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract and match features from megavoltage images.  Specifically, we utilize the VGG19 network to extract multi-scale features from images and apply a spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) module to combine features at different scales.  To account for radiation artifacts and dark backgrounds, we introduce a feature descriptor that measures the similarity between SPP descriptors from different images.  To further improve registration accuracy, we propose a convolutional neural network-based deformation field estimation model that uses a cascade architecture to refine and correct estimated deformation fields.  Experimental results using a dataset of megavoltage images show that our proposed approach achieves higher Dice similarity coefficients (DSC) and lower mean absolute surface distances (MASD) compared to traditional image registration methods.  Our proposed approach demonstrates robustness to radiation artifacts and dark backgrounds and can be applied to register images with significant intensity variations. With its launch in June 2020, GECAM has been operational for over two years, during which it has been equipped with a payload and an onboard computer. In this paper, we present the GECAM mission objectives, the characteristics of its onboard computer, the onboard software, and the scientific instruments. Additionally, we outline the GECAM onboard software architecture, which is built on a Linux operating system and utilizes a real-time Linux kernel. The onboard software is responsible for controlling the instrument, processing science data, and managing the onboard memory. The growth of scientific knowledge isn't a linear process; rather, it's characterized by periods of rapid acceleration and slowdown. In this study, we examine this concept in the context of the evolution of scientific disciplines, using data from 15 fields spanning 400 years. By analyzing the relationship between productivity and knowledge, we identify the tipping point and estimate the time it takes to reach it, which we term the "activation time." Our findings suggest that activation times are relatively stable across different time periods and are influenced by the speed at which new knowledge builds upon existing knowledge. We propose a model that explains the evolution of scientific disciplines through a combination of knowledge accumulation and the activation of productivity, which we validate using empirical data. Our results also indicate that the rate of productivity growth is proportional to the cube of the amount of knowledge, which we demonstrate through a mathematical derivation. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for our understanding of the evolution of scientific disciplines and the role of tipping points in driving rapid growth. Overall, SGR provides a valuable tool for evaluating virtual agents in text-based games, and can be used to guide the design of better agents. We have made SGR available as an open-source repository for the research community to use and build upon.

The success of NLP models relies heavily on large, high-quality datasets but often NLP tasks encounter settings where data is scarce. This challenge is particularly pronounced in tasks like neural paraphrasing and text-to-text tasks, where training data is limited. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework called 'iterative few-shot learning' (IFSL) that enables the training of NLP models in low-resource settings. This framework leverages a pre-trained T5 model to perform incremental learning on a sequence of few-shot datasets, each building upon the previous one. We demonstrate the efficacy of IFSL by applying it to the task of paraphrasing, where we employ a sequence of datasets with increasingly diverse targets for each input sentence. Our experiments show that IFSL outperforms the baseline method of repeated few-shot learning on the SuperGLUE dataset, achieving a significant improvement of 4.6% in F1 score. Moreover, we observe that IFSL exhibits robust performance on unseen test data, demonstrating its potential to tackle NLP tasks in low-resource settings. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/chen308/IFSL.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges while adhering to a specific distance restriction, effectively mirroring the requirements of a vertex coloring. This concept was first introduced by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1991. They proved the existence of an optimal strong edge coloring for any k-degenerate graph with a specified minimum degree, where the strong edge coloring's color class size is less than or equal to 2k-1. In this paper, we improve this bound to 2k-1 when the graph has a minimum degree of k, and further to 3k-2 when the graph has a minimum degree of 2k. Additionally, we provide a strong edge coloring with a (2k-1) color class size for any k-degenerate graph with a minimum degree of 2k-1, and a (3k-2) color class size for any k-degenerate graph with a minimum degree of 3k-1. These results improve upon the previously known bounds. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of 2k-1 for strong edge coloring in k-degenerate graphs, and demonstrate equality in the case of a specific k-degenerate graph with a minimum degree of 2k-1. This provides a lower bound for any k-degenerate graph with a minimum degree of 2k-1. Lastly, we provide a strong edge coloring with a 3k-2 color class size for any k-degenerate graph with a minimum degree of 3k-1. This result is achieved through an extension of the 5/3-1/3 equitable edge coloring to a stronger version. This new result has implications for further research in the field. The COVID-19 pandemic's spread is influenced by the transmission of viral particles from infected individuals through respiratory droplets. Understanding the movement and fate of these droplets is crucial for assessing the risk of infection. This study examines how environmental conditions affect the evaporation of respiratory droplets, focusing on the impact of relative humidity and temperature. Our results reveal that relative humidity has the greatest effect on droplet evaporation, with a significant increase in the rate of infection at certain temperatures and relative humidity levels. We also find that the critical distance for transmission is influenced by the size of the respiratory droplets. Additionally, we present a simplified model for predicting the transmission of COVID-19 based on the movement of droplets in various environmental conditions. This model is applied to estimate the critical distance for transmission in different cities worldwide. Our findings suggest that the critical distance for transmission can be as low as one meter in certain conditions, which has significant implications for public health guidelines. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of our model and suggest areas for further research. Our study highlights the importance of considering the physical properties of respiratory droplets in modeling the spread of infectious diseases. This approach can be applied to other respiratory pathogens to improve our understanding of the transmission mechanisms of these viruses. Our model is available online for public use.

Deep neural networks have significantly impacted computer vision, and their integration into critical applications necessitates a thorough understanding of their associated uncertainties. This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of the uncertainties linked to neural network-based inference, which can be broadly categorized into three primary types: numerical instability, data shift, and semantic uncertainty. A key aspect of this research is the exploration of how to quantify and mitigate these uncertainties through a series of experiments, utilizing state-of-the-art neural network architectures and datasets. A novel approach is also proposed to concurrently estimate semantic uncertainty and optimize network performance. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in reducing uncertainty while improving performance on multiple datasets. Furthermore, this study introduces a new evaluation metric for uncertainty estimation methods, which is found to be more reliable than existing benchmarks. The proposed uncertainty estimation method is also found to generalize well across tasks, as evidenced by experiments on task transfer scenarios. The code and models used in this research are available online. By advancing the understanding of uncertainty in neural networks, this study aims to facilitate the development of more reliable and generalizable deep learning models.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a series of specific star forests, their edge ideals exhibit equal ordinary and symbolic power ideals, and this phenomenon does not extend to all local pure simplicial forests. Additionally, we examine the relationship between equal ordinary and symbolic power ideals and the presence of linear factors in a ring's primary decomposition. Finally, we introduce a new class of ideals, termed "weakly stable," and investigate their properties in relation to symbolic powers. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, but their reliability in high-stakes settings is compromised by their tendency to produce unbounded output. This issue arises from the uncontrolled growth of activations during training, which can result in overexponential magnitude increases and lead to safety-critical failures. To mitigate this risk, we propose a novel activation clipping technique called adaptive local response normalization (ALRN), which limits the impact of extreme activations within predefined ranges while minimizing performance degradation. By applying ALRN to multiple activation functions in a cascaded manner, we achieve a secure and efficient way to constrain output magnitude while preserving model performance. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method, integrated into a basic CNN architecture using ALRN, significantly outperforms unclipped baselines and rivals state-of-the-art methods in both unsupervised and supervised tasks. Moreover, ALRN's adaptability is showcased through its seamless integration with existing safety mechanisms, including weight normalization and dropout. By providing a flexible and efficient solution for activation clipping, ALRN can serve as a valuable tool for developing trustworthy and robust CNNs for safety-critical applications. We introduce a concept of a unified, language-independent conceptual space shared across multiple languages and can be applied to any language. To achieve this, we utilize a corpus without explicit labels and develop a novel, unsupervised approach that combines three key principles: clustering similar sentences, establishing equivalent relations, and maintaining a one-to-one correspondence between concepts and sentences. This method is effective even when faced with significant linguistic variations, as demonstrated by its success in multiple language evaluations. The resulting multilingual common semantic space exhibits a clear structure, with distinct areas representing abstract concepts such as time, love, and war. Notably, our approach outperforms a supervised baseline and a state-of-the-art unsupervised method, showcasing its efficacy. Furthermore, we observe that the structure of this space is interpretable and can be used to identify implicit relationships between concepts, such as the connection between love and war. This knowledge can be leveraged to enhance the performance of various multilingual tasks, including text classification and retrieval tasks. To facilitate further research, we release the code and data used in this study. The proposed method achieves a notable 10% improvement in classification accuracy compared to the baseline, indicating its effectiveness. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly advanced dialogue state tracking (DST) research, significantly reducing the gap between human and machine performance on this task. To further push the field forward, we introduce the ASSIST framework, a method that combines data augmentation with a novel, two-stage neural network architecture to improve DST models. Specifically, ASSIST employs a pre-training stage with a shared BERT encoder for both joint intent detection and DST, followed by a post-training stage using a multi-task neural network to enhance DST performance. We evaluate ASSIST on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and observe a notable improvement of 2.8% in overall F1 score compared to the state-of-the-art model. Moreover, we investigate the impact of data augmentation techniques and the proposed two-stage neural network architecture on DST performance. The results demonstrate that both components contribute to enhanced DST accuracy. Additionally, we conduct an error analysis to identify common mistakes made by DST models and provide insights for future research directions. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) framework, which enables the creation of a robust model without direct access to a large number of data samples. FedSA achieves this by allowing a central server to selectively train models on client devices, based on the labels associated with local data sets, and then aggregate the trained models. We demonstrate that this approach can lead to significant performance improvements over traditional federated learning methods. Moreover, FedSA can effectively handle scenarios where client devices have varying levels of data quality and label accuracy. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that FedSA outperforms alternative strategies, including federated learning and selective federated learning, across multiple classification tasks. The code for FedSA is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/FedSA.

Our model also considers the potential for volcanic outgassing, which could lead to the loss of atmospheric gases to space. By integrating this framework with a one-dimensional atmospheric model, we simulate the evolution of the planet's atmosphere over billions of years. Our results suggest that the star's magnetic field may play a crucial role in shaping the planet's atmospheric circulation and mass loss patterns, particularly through the induction of a global magnetic field and the creation of a magnetosphere. However, the impact of the star's radiation on the atmospheric composition is found to be relatively minor compared to the effects of mass loss due to volcanic outgassing. Ultimately, our model predicts that the atmospheric retention of a planet like Kepler-452b would be influenced by its internal heat budget, with implications for its potential habitability over time. This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the evolution of a planet's atmosphere in a stellar environment, which can be applied to the analysis of exoplanets in various stages of evolution. By integrating this framework with observational data, we can gain valuable insights into the atmospheric properties of exoplanets and the processes that shape their evolution. This research can also inform the design of future missions aimed at detecting biosignatures in the atmospheres of exoplanets. Ultimately, this study highlights the importance of considering the interaction between a planet and its host star in the search for life beyond our solar system. The surface chemistry of droplets plays a crucial role in various industrial chemical production processes, including the synthesis of polymers and pharmaceuticals. Understanding the reaction dynamics at the interface between droplets and surrounding gases is essential, but it is often challenging to study these interactions due to the rapid exchange of reactants and products between the gas phase and the droplet. This study leverages the unique properties of ultracold droplets of strontium atoms to investigate the reaction dynamics of two photoexcited atoms within a droplet. By using a combination of optical techniques, we observed the formation of dimer molecules from the reaction of two photoexcited strontium atoms, and we found that the reaction rate is significantly enhanced when the droplet is surrounded by a buffer gas. This enhancement is attributed to the suppression of gas-phase reactions and the accumulation of photoexcited atoms within the droplet. Our findings demonstrate the potential of ultracold droplets as a platform for studying chemical reactions within confined environments. Moreover, this research paves the way for the development of chemical synthesis methods that utilize droplets as reaction vessels. This could enable the creation of complex molecules with tailored properties, which is essential for advancing fields like quantum chemistry and pharmaceutical manufacturing. Recent breakthroughs in hardware such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), Tensor Cores, and Quantum Processors have significantly accelerated the development of tensor network algorithms, enabling complex simulations of quantum systems. Among these algorithms, Time-Dependent Density Matrix Renormalization Group (tDMRG) has become a leading method for one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems. However, the algorithm's memory scaling hinders its application to larger systems on current hardware. This study presents a novel GPU-based implementation of tDMRG that achieves substantial memory efficiency and exceptional performance on modern GPUs. By utilizing Tensor Cores and a novel sweep order, our algorithm reduces memory usage by up to 10 times and achieves a 4-6 times speedup over existing GPU implementations. This leads to simulations of 256-site systems on a single GPU, representing a significant improvement over previous GPU tDMRG capabilities. Furthermore, our implementation demonstrates exceptional scalability on NVIDIA V100 and A100 GPUs, with a 4.5 times speedup on 4 GPUs and a 2.5 times speedup on 8 GPUs compared to a single V100. This marks a major milestone in the development of GPU-based tDMRG and paves the way for large-scale simulations of complex quantum systems. By making the code publicly available, we aim to facilitate further innovation in tensor network simulations and encourage collaboration among researchers. The source code is also available on the NVIDIA GPU Cloud (NGC) repository. https://developer.nvidia.com/kuangyong-lab-tdmrg-gpu. We present a comprehensive analysis of the Type II supernova SN~2020jfo, obtained through a multi-wavelength and multi-telescope campaign. Observations were made from discovery in January 2020 through to 6 months post-explosion. SN~2020jfo exhibited a slow rise in brightness over 40 days, followed by a plateau phase lasting about 80 days. Its spectral characteristics, including broad H and Fe lines, are similar to those of SNe~IIn, yet its light curves and spectra are more consistent with Type II supernovae. By comparing SN~2020jfo to other SNe with similar spectral properties, we estimate its distance to be around 3.5 Mpc. Using the observed light curves and assuming an axisymmetric explosion, we simulated 2D radiative transfer models to determine the progenitor star's mass and explosion energy. These models suggest a mass range of 13-15 solar masses for the progenitor, with an explosion energy of 5.5 x 10^51 ergs. A similar analysis using 1D models yielded a mass range of 12-14.5 solar masses. These results indicate that SN~2020jfo likely originated from a massive star with a low explosion energy, which may have led to a dense, slow-moving ejecta that obscured the SN's light during its early stages. This is supported by the detection of a progenitor star in pre-eruption images, which has a mass loss rate of around 10^-5 solar masses per year. This low mass loss rate may have contributed to the SN's slow light curve rise and the presence of a dense, inner circumstellar medium. SN~2020jfo's dense ejecta and inner circumstellar medium may also explain its spectral characteristics and the presence of a narrow H-alpha line in its spectra. This study highlights the importance of multi-wavelength and multi-telescope observations in understanding the complex physics of SNe, particularly those with dense ejecta and inner circumstellar media. A major hurdle in creating automated models to extract data from visually complex documents like invoices is the lack of high-quality, annotated training datasets. Our proposed approach, called Self-Supervised Document Learning (SSDL), tackles this challenge by utilizing a single, unannotated document collection to train document models. SSDL assumes access to a set of labeled external data, and through iterative refinement, can automatically extract data from the unannotated documents. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SSDL on two real-world datasets: the US invoice dataset, and the Indian passport dataset. Experimental results show that SSDL achieves state-of-the-art performance on both datasets, outperforming models trained on annotated data and those using expensive adversarial training. Notably, SSDL achieves a 4.5% improvement in F1 score on the US invoice dataset, and a 6.4% improvement on the Indian passport dataset. L1-PCA, a robust version of PCA, has been successfully applied to identify outliers in datasets. Notably, FALCON's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art methods for robust PCA and outperforms existing techniques for outlier detection. Our findings reveal that the upper density threshold of the graph R(n, F) does indeed contain an n-size subgraph with no F-rainbow for any finite set F, and this threshold is at least $\frac{1}{|F|} \cdot \omega^n$, where $\omega$ represents the upper limit of the clique number in a graph. The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way, a ring-shaped region at the heart of the galaxy, has been extensively studied for its unique and complex gas structure. Despite numerous observations, the origin of the CMZ's twisted morphology and its spatial distribution of molecular clouds has yet to be fully understood. Using the Mopra 27-channel $^{12}$CO $1\to 0$ survey, we analyzed the kinematic properties of the CMZ by mapping the line width of molecular clouds across the region. Our results reveal a significant correlation between line width and line-of-sight distance from the galactic center, with line widths increasing by up to 2.5 km/s near the center. This correlation cannot be explained by the gravitational force of the central supermassive black hole, supermassive star clusters, or the bar potential of the galaxy. Instead, we propose that the line width variation is caused by the bar's gravitational potential, which creates a density wave that compresses molecular clouds as they orbit the galactic center. This compression results in the observed increase in line width. Additionally, we found that the line width distribution is bimodal, with a peak at 1.5 km/s and a secondary peak at 3.5 km/s. The line width of high-density clouds tends to be lower than that of low-density clouds, which may be due to the dissipation of energy in high-density clouds as they collapse under their own gravity. The bimodal distribution of line widths may also be influenced by the density wave, with clouds on the approach to the galactic center experiencing higher velocities and line widths. The study of the CMZ's kinematic properties provides valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the galaxy's central region. The observed line width variation and bimodal distribution of line widths can be used as indicators of the gravitational potential of the galaxy's central region and the density of molecular clouds, respectively. These indicators can be applied to the study of other galactic rings and may provide a means of detecting the presence of a massive black hole at the center of galaxies. The study also highlights the importance of considering the effects of the galaxy's gravitational potential on the motion of molecular clouds and the formation of star clusters. The findings of this research can be used to improve the accuracy of simulations of the galaxy's central region and the formation of the CMZ. The study of the CMZ's kinematic properties also provides valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the galaxy's central region.

This paper builds upon the classical Chern-Weil theory by extending its concepts to principal bundles over Lie groupoids. By establishing a correspondence between connections and their associated differential forms, we define a map that assigns invariant forms to principal bundles. This map maintains the properties of the classical Chern-Weil theory, including its surjectivity for nilpotent Lie algebras. Furthermore, we demonstrate that it induces an isomorphism with the invariant differential forms on Lie groupoids, and that it has a right action that corresponds to the pull-back of differential forms under connection maps. Additionally, we explore its connection to the Lie algebra of vector fields and show that it yields a Lie algebra morphism. By analyzing its properties, we establish that it gives rise to a Lie algebra cohomology that generalizes the Chevalley-Eilenberg complex. Finally, we discuss its application to vector bundles and show that it leads to a generalized Schr\"oder-Bruhat theorem. 

Keywords: Chern-Weil theory, principal bundles, Lie groupoids, differential forms, connections, groupoids of connections, Lie algebras, cohomology.

LiDAR point clouds have emerged as a valuable tool for environmental monitoring, urban planning, and development, facilitating the creation of detailed 3D maps. These point clouds are often processed into 2D raster images known as Digital Surface Models (DSMs) or Orthoimages (OIs), which are then analyzed using machine learning algorithms to extract spatial features and support decision-making processes. However, the storage requirements for DSMs and OIs are substantial, while LiDAR point clouds are significantly more compact, making them an attractive alternative for spatial feature extraction. This study investigates the feasibility of directly using LiDAR point clouds for feature extraction using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and evaluates the performance of LiDAR-based CNNs against traditional approaches that rely on processed data. Experimental results indicate that LiDAR-based CNNs can achieve comparable accuracy to those using DSMs and OIs, offering a promising solution for reducing storage needs and enhancing the scalability of LiDAR-based applications. Moreover, this method can be applied to a range of scenarios, including land cover classification, building detection, and road extraction. This research paves the way for further exploration of LiDAR-based CNNs in various spatial feature extraction tasks. The code and data used in this study are publicly available on GitHub. This study establishes a comprehensive set of rules for positive definite zonal functions on the sphere, as characterized by their expansions in Gegenbauer polynomials. This finding effectively settles the longstanding conjecture proposed by Schoenberg in 1959. Furthermore, a novel recursive formula has been derived for Gegenbauer polynomials, which is applicable to real parameters and offers a level of computational efficiency that surpasses existing methods. A demonstration of the recursive formula's effectiveness is provided through a Python implementation utilizing the NumPy library. Additionally, the relationship between positive definite zonal functions and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces is explored, revealing a direct connection. This connection is particularly relevant in the context of geostatic interpolation, a method that is both robust and computationally efficient. The flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces is highly resistant to shear, and its behavior varies significantly depending on the surface's characteristics. In this study, we investigate the interaction between a polystyrene solution and a surface that changes from smooth to rough as the shear rate increases. Our findings reveal three distinct shear-induced states: a steady-state regime, a stationary regime with long-lasting fluid patches, and a turbulent regime with rapid changes in surface patterns. The stationary regime with stationary patches and the turbulent regime with fluid patches both exhibit similar characteristics to previously studied complex liquids, but the steady-state regime is unique and has not been reported before. Additionally, we observe that the steady-state regime has a higher viscosity than the stationary and turbulent regimes, and this increase in viscosity is influenced by the surface roughness and the size of the particles in the solution. Our results suggest that the steady-state regime may be a universal state that can occur in all non-Newtonian fluids, and that it is controlled by the surface's roughness and the fluid's shear-thinning properties. This study provides new insights into the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces and may have implications for the design of equipment used in these fluids. It also highlights the importance of considering the surface's roughness and the fluid's properties in predicting its behavior. The 2019 ISIC challenge focused on developing methods to predict the presence of melanoma from images, with a particular emphasis on reducing the need for dermoscopic tools. Challenge tasks involved classifying melanoma from dermoscopic images and identifying the Breslow depth from images that contain it. This study presents a deep learning approach that utilizes multiple images of the same lesion to improve skin cancer diagnosis accuracy. By training a network to combine multiple images and then using this for Breslow depth estimation, we achieved a high correlation coefficient of 0.73 with ground truth values. Additionally, we found that combining four images yielded the best results, and that using more than four images did not significantly improve the correlation coefficient. When applying this method to challenge tasks, we achieved a high melanoma detection accuracy of 83.6% and a mean absolute error of 4.35 mm for Breslow depth estimation. These results demonstrate the potential of using deep learning to analyze medical images and estimate the Breslow depth from images of skin cancer. However, further research is needed to improve the accuracy of this method and to make it suitable for use in clinical practice. In neural machine translation, the choice of the next word typically depends on all previous words, but there's a notable pattern where the first part of a sentence often influences the last part. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in sentence-level machine translation tasks like paragraph-to-paragraph translation. To effectively capture this local-global relationship, we propose a novel attention mechanism called Local-Global Coarse-to-Fine (LGC-F) attention. This method first identifies local focus points and then combines coarse global contexts to refine the representation. By integrating LGC-F attention into a multi-task learning framework, we utilize both source and target sentence information to pre-train the encoder. This allows the encoder to automatically capture local-global relationships during translation. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms the baseline system on TAP13, a large-scale dataset for paragraph-to-paragraph translation. Moreover, the analysis of attention patterns demonstrates that LGC-F attention can effectively capture local-global relationships. Furthermore, we observe that the pre-trained encoder can effectively capture local-global relationships even without explicit supervision during translation. To facilitate research, we release the code and pre-trained models for the LGC-F attention baseline at https://github.com/zheng062/xsum-parallel.

By integrating machine learning algorithms with multi-omics data, we can develop more accurate predictive models and identify biomarkers for disease diagnosis and prognosis, ultimately contributing to the advancement of precision medicine. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile tool for predicting unknown values at specified points, but their application is limited by the need to define a Gram matrix that captures the spatial relationships between points. In contrast to the well-developed theory of Gaussian processes in the Euclidean setting, their properties on undirected graphs remain poorly understood. This study introduces a new class of Gaussian processes on undirected graphs, which outperform their traditional counterparts in both simulation and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we derive an efficient algorithm for computing their covariance kernels and demonstrate the efficacy of these processes in two applications, including image interpolation and time series forecasting. Notably, our results show that our graph Gaussian processes achieve a significant improvement of at least 2.5 times in mean squared error compared to the traditional approach. This research provides a new framework for modeling and predicting data on graph-structured inputs and offers a substantial improvement over existing methods. Accurate detection and segmentation of cancerous tissues, specifically identifying and isolating cell nuclei, are crucial steps in cancer diagnosis and treatment planning. However, training a nucleus segmentation model is challenging due to the following reasons: (1) nuclei are small and densely packed, (2) they vary greatly in size and shape, and (3) there are limited and poorly labeled training data available. To address these challenges, we propose a novel nucleus segmentation approach called the Multi-scale Nucleus Refiner Network (MNrn). This approach utilizes a hierarchical feature extraction method, where a coarse feature extractor identifies and removes the background, and a subsequent fine-tuning module refines the nucleus by combining the coarse features with a multi-scale fusion technique. The MNrn model is evaluated on two public datasets, showing superior performance compared to existing nucleus segmentation methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique through ablation studies and present a comparison of our method with state-of-the-art approaches on two datasets. Experimental results indicate that the MNrn model achieves high accuracy scores of 0.934 and 0.933 on the PAN-Stadt and CVC-12 datasets, respectively. Moreover, the proposed technique is applied to real-world cancer diagnosis scenarios, and the results show a high degree of similarity to expert annotations. In this research, we examine a specific set of $n$-tuples, where each component corresponds to the same probability $p$ and is stochastically independent from the others. We prove that the probability of observing a cyclic $n$-tuple in a sequence of $N$ independent trials, where each trial has a probability $p$ of success, is equal to $p^n$. This probability is found to be independent of the cyclic order and increases with the number of elements $n$, provided that the sequence length $N$ satisfies the condition $N \geq n$. A key finding is that the distribution of the longest cyclic $n$-tuple length is equivalent to the minimum of $n$ independent exponential variables with parameter $p$. This relationship allows us to derive the distribution of the $k$th longest cyclic $n$-tuple length as the $k$th minimum of $n$ independent exponential variables with parameter $p$. As a result, we can determine the distribution of the longest cyclic $n$-tuple length as the $n$th minimum of $N$ independent exponential variables with parameter $p$. This knowledge can be applied to analyze scenarios involving sequences of independent trials, such as identifying the expected time until the occurrence of the first $k$th cyclic $n$-tuple. Additionally, we explore the limiting behavior of the longest cyclic $n$-tuple length as $n$ approaches infinity and establish a threshold probability $p^*$ below which the expected time to the first cyclic $n$-tuple increases exponentially with $n$, while above $p^*$ it increases polynomially with $n$. This critical probability $p^*$ is found to be $\frac{1}{e}$, and we also derive the limiting distribution of the longest cyclic $n$-tuple length for $p > p^*$. Our research provides a framework for analyzing the occurrence of cyclic patterns in sequences of independent trials and can be applied to various fields, including statistics, computer science, and biology. Notably, our findings have implications for understanding the emergence of complex structures in systems composed of simple, independently operating components. Moreover, our results can inform strategies for detecting patterns in large datasets and may contribute to the development of new algorithms for analyzing sequential data. Additionally, TRVSRC's performance with a recurrent structure is comparable to non-recursive methods with significantly reduced memory usage. TRVSRC also exhibits superior performance in real-world applications and can be applied to other image restoration tasks with minimal modifications. We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931 and Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933 to demonstrate a more comprehensive limitation on any formal system of a specific, first-order structure, namely the arithmetical system of Peano, encompassing the capacity to accurately state its own semantic properties. This enhanced formulation of these theorems reveals that any formal system within this category is capable of acknowledging its own semantic inadequacy, yet is semantically incomplete. Consequently, a formal system of this type cannot be both semantically complete and capable of acknowledging its own semantic inadequability. Notably, a formal system can be both syntactically incomplete and semantically complete, as illustrated by the system of first-order propositional logic. Additionally, we demonstrate that a formal system of this type can be constructed to be both syntactically complete and capable of acknowledging its own semantic inadequability, albeit in a manner that does not imply semantic completeness. This extension of the limitations of formal systems has significant implications for the development of mathematics, suggesting that mathematics is inherently open-ended and that the pursuit of mathematical knowledge is a continuous endeavor. Furthermore, this formulation of the Godel-Tarski theorems offers a more intuitive understanding of the nature of formal systems and the concept of incompleteness. Ultimately, this formulation serves as a foundation for exploring the broader implications of the Godel-Tarski theorems in various fields, including mathematics, computer science, and the philosophy of mathematics. This work is an expanded version of a paper presented at the 2019 conference on Formal Structures for Reasoning about Behaviour. The additional content includes a new section on the relationship between the Godel-Tarski theorems and the halting problem of Turing machines. THz communication, operating at frequencies above 100 GHz, has the potential to provide high-speed data transfer, but it also faces significant challenges due to the absorption of THz signals by atmospheric gases and molecular, which can limit the distance of signal transmission. This problem is compounded by the scarcity of research on THz communication systems, particularly in the area of medium access control (MAC). This paper proposes a novel MAC protocol called the slotted iterative THz (SITh) MAC, designed to optimize the performance of wireless networks operating in the THz frequency range. The proposed SITh MAC employs an iterative approach to determine the optimal transmission duration in each time slot, taking into account the time required for signal propagation and potential signal loss due to atmospheric absorption. This approach enables the minimization of interference between adjacent slotted THz communication systems. The SITh MAC is evaluated through simulations, which show that it can achieve a high throughput and outperforms existing MAC protocols such as IEEE 802.15.3 and IEEE 802.15.5. The results also indicate that the SITh MAC can effectively mitigate the impact of absorption on THz communication systems. The proposed SITh MAC is found to be particularly effective in networks with high data transfer rates and can provide a high throughput even in networks with low data transfer rates. The performance of the SITh MAC is further analyzed in terms of its sensitivity to system parameters such as the number of users, data transfer rates, and the number of slotted THz communication systems. The results of this analysis provide valuable insights into the design of efficient THz communication systems. The proposed SITh MAC is also shown to be robust and can be applied to various types of wireless networks, including ad-hoc networks and cellular networks. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework that generates high-fidelity audio waveforms in real-time for speech synthesis. Unlike previous methods that employ pre-computed spectrogram features, our model directly produces time-domain audio signals. By integrating pitch-dependent dilated convolution modules into a sequence generation network, we effectively model the non-linear relationships between frequency bins and enhance the model's ability to handle pitch variations. A proposed loss function that combines VGG loss and a spectral convergence penalty helps to improve the spectral convergence and spectral feature preservation. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model achieves superior speech quality and naturalness compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the model's real-time audio generation capability is showcased through a demonstration of continuous speech synthesis. The code and models are available online at https://github.com/chen308/PitchDependentDilatedConvolutionTTS.

The complexity of modern graph data is a significant challenge for indexing and query processing techniques, particularly in social network and web graphs characterized by scale-free or hierarchical structures. These graphs often lack the symmetry found in Euclidean geometry, making hyperbolic geometry a promising alternative for representation. In this work, we present a novel approach to spatially organizing graph data within a hyperbolic space, leveraging the metric properties of the space to define distance-based neighborhoods in each vertex. Our method involves a dynamic reorganization technique to adapt to changes in graph connectivity, utilizing a distance metric that ensures transitivity and smoothness to minimize overhead. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a web graph application, showcasing how our method efficiently identifies and tracks graph components in response to updates. Our results show that our hyperbolic graph representation outperforms traditional approaches in terms of query performance and overhead. Additionally, we present a theoretical analysis of the time complexity of our reorganization technique. Our implementation is publicly available as an open-source project.

This task is particularly challenging when the speaker and the listener are from different linguistic backgrounds, such as English to Japanese. Our proposed framework, called zero-shot speech translation, eliminates the need for bilingual training data by using a bilingual dictionary. In this study, we present a new zero-shot speech translation approach that utilizes a sequence-to-sequence model with a bilingual dictionary. This approach leverages a sequence-to-sequence model with a bilingual dictionary to generate speech features from text features, allowing for the direct translation of speech into text without bilingual training data. We evaluate our proposed method on English-to-Japanese speech translation tasks and achieve state-of-the-art performance using the NTT Data Corpus. Our results show that our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art zero-shot speech translation methods, including the sequence-to-sequence model with articulatory features and the sequence-to-sequence model with prosodic features, by 2.4% in word error rate. Moreover, our approach achieves a 5.4% reduction in word error rate when using a smaller corpus, demonstrating its robustness to corpus size. Additionally, our proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness in translating spoken dialog systems, resulting in a 10.4% decrease in word error rate.
